uni-llb-moot-court.title: Moot Court, Trial Observation & Pre-Trial Preparation (Scenario Labs)
uni-llb-moot-court.description: Moot problem analysis, legal research, memorial drafting, oral advocacy, client interviewing, trial observation diaries and full scenario moot labs in constitutional, criminal and commercial law. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian LLB programmes. Fictional problems for practice only.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Reading a Moot Problem and Legal Research
courses.summary: How moot competitions work, dissecting the moot proposition, framing issues, building a research plan with primary and secondary sources, reading judgments efficiently and citing them correctly.
outcomes: Extract facts, parties, forum and issues from a moot proposition
Frame issues as neutral legal questions
Plan research across statutes, cases and secondary sources
Brief a judgment using ratio and obiter correctly

scenes.text: You receive a 6-page fictional problem set in the 'Supreme Court of Indiana'. Memorials are due in four weeks.
Then you will argue for 20 minutes before three judges. Where do you begin?

steps.title: Structure of a moot
steps.body:
- **Moot proposition**: fictional facts, often set in a fictional country whose laws are 'pari materia' with Indian law.
- **Teams**: 2 speakers + 1 researcher; you may argue for petitioner/appellant or respondent.
- **Written submissions (memorial)** filed by deadline; scored separately.
- **Oral rounds**: preliminary, quarter-final, semi-final, final; time per speaker (often 15–20 minutes) plus rebuttal/sur-rebuttal.
- **Marking**: knowledge of law, application to facts, structure, responses to questions, court manners, time management.

steps.title: BCI practical paper
steps.body: University 'Moot Court Exercise and Internship' papers commonly assess: three moot courts, observation of trial (civil and criminal), interviewing techniques and pre-trial preparation, and a viva voce. Keep a diary of court visits and client interviews.

steps.title: First 48 hours
steps.body: Read the problem three times: once for the story, once to list facts, once to spot legal issues and ambiguities. Send clarification questions before the deadline set by organisers.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Adding facts not in the problem. Moot judges penalise assumptions; argue only from the given facts and reasonable inferences.

Research and build arguments for both sides

scenes.text: Moot facts: the State of Mahanagar (Republic of Indiana) bans all protests within 2 km of its Secretariat after a violent protest; a farmers' union is denied permission for a peaceful sit-in.
The union files a writ in the High Court, loses, and appeals to the Supreme Court of Indiana.

steps.title: Fact matrix
steps.body: Parties: Farmers' Union (Appellant) v State of Mahanagar (Respondent). Forum: Supreme Court of Indiana (appeal from High Court writ). Key facts: (1) Violent protest on 3 January led to injuries; (2) Notification dated 10 January bans all gatherings within 2 km for an indefinite period; (3) Union applied for a peaceful sit-in of 200 persons on 20 January; (4) Permission refused citing the ban; (5) An alternative site 12 km away was offered.

steps.title: Issues framed (neutral)
steps.body:
1. Whether the appeal is maintainable before the Supreme Court of Indiana.
2. Whether the blanket ban notification violates Article 19(1)(a) and (b) and is not saved by Article 19(2) and (3).
3. Whether the refusal of permission was arbitrary under Article 14.
4. Whether the offer of an alternative site cures the restriction.
Authorities to research: Himat Lal K. Shah v Commissioner of Police (1973); Ramlila Maidan Incident (2012); Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan v Union of India (2018) – Jantar Mantar; Anuradha Bhasin v Union of India (2020) – proportionality and Section 144 orders; Amit Sahni v Commissioner of Police (2020) – Shaheen Bagh, public places cannot be occupied indefinitely.

steps.title: Neutral phrasing
steps.body: Use 'Whether…' questions in the memorial's issues section; argue your side in the arguments, not in the issues.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Forgetting maintainability. Always consider jurisdiction first.

Indefinite duration of the ban
Ban covers peaceful and violent gatherings alike
No reasons recorded for refusing the union
Alternative site 12 km away

quiz.why: Neutral issues show the court the questions to be decided; advocacy follows in the arguments.

quiz.q: Which case concerned protests at Jantar Mantar?
quiz.why: The Supreme Court held a complete ban on protests at Jantar Mantar was unreasonable and called for regulation.

quiz.q: Anuradha Bhasin (2020) is useful because it applied
options: Proportionality to restrictions including prohibitory orders
quiz.why: It required restrictions on rights to be necessary, proportionate and reviewable.

scenes.text: A database search for 'freedom of assembly' returns 3,000 results.
How do you find the ten that matter?

steps.title: Research ladder
steps.body:
1. **Secondary sources first**: commentaries (e.g. M.P. Jain on Constitutional Law, D.D. Basu), law review articles – for the map of the law.
2. **Primary sources**: Constitution, bare Acts (official India Code), rules and notifications.
3. **Leading cases**: Constitution Bench and larger bench decisions; check whether overruled or distinguished.
4. **Foreign authorities** only if persuasive and the problem invites them.
5. Databases: SCC Online, Manupatra, official Supreme Court/High Court websites, Indian Kanoon (free; verify text against official reports).

steps.title: Search techniques
steps.body: Boolean operators (AND, OR, NOT), phrase search ("freedom of assembly"), proximity (protest /5 ban), filters by court and bench strength, 'cited by' to find later treatment. Keep a research log: source, proposition, pin-point paragraph.

steps.title: Worked search
steps.body: Query: "Article 19(1)(b)" AND (protest OR demonstration) AND (ban OR prohibition) – filter: Supreme Court, 2010–2025. Then use 'cited by' on Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan to find later cases.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Citing a case without checking if it was overruled. Always check subsequent history.

items: Read a commentary for the overview
Read the bare provisions
Identify leading cases
Check subsequent history of each case
Note pin-point paragraphs in a research log
Look for counter-authorities for the other side

quiz.q: Why start with secondary sources?
options: They give a map of the law and leading cases
quiz.why: Commentaries summarise the field and point to key authorities quickly.

quiz.q: A Boolean search with AND
quiz.why: AND narrows results to documents containing every term.

quiz.q: Before citing, always check
options: Whether the case was overruled or distinguished
quiz.why: An overruled authority is no longer good law and damages credibility.

lessons.title: Lab: Brief a judgment and cite correctly

scenes.text: You must summarise a 200-page Constitution Bench judgment in one page for your team.
What is the ratio and what is merely obiter?

steps.title: Case brief template
steps.body:
1. Citation and bench.
2. Facts (short).
3. Issues.
4. Holding (answer to each issue).
5. **Ratio decidendi**: the principle necessary for the decision (binding under Article 141).
6. **Obiter dicta**: observations not necessary for the decision (persuasive).
7. Concurring/dissenting opinions.
8. Relevance to your moot (which side, which issue).

steps.title: Citation style
steps.body: Follow the competition's rules (often a uniform style such as Bluebook or OSCOLA, or an Indian style). Typical Indian format: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India, (1978) 1 SCC 248 ¶ 7. Use pin-point paragraphs; use 'Id.'/'Ibid.' per the style; list authorities in an Index of Authorities.

steps.title: Brief extract
steps.body: Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan v. Union of India, (2018) 17 SCC 324 (2 judges). Issue: whether a complete ban on demonstrations at Jantar Mantar/Boat Club is valid. Holding: no; right to protest is part of Art. 19(1)(a)/(b); authorities must balance with residents' rights and frame guidelines for regulated use. Ratio: a blanket, indefinite ban on peaceful protest in an area is disproportionate where regulation can achieve the aim. Use: Appellant, Issue 2.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Quoting a dissent or obiter as if it were the ratio. Label persuasive material honestly.

items.text: Principle necessary to decide the issue before the court
Passing remark on a hypothetical situation
Dissenting judge's reasoning
Majority's answer to the question referred

quiz.q: Under Article 141 what binds lower courts?
options: The ratio decidendi of the Supreme Court
quiz.why: Article 141 makes the law declared, i.e. the ratio, binding on all courts in India.

quiz.q: A pin-point citation refers to
options: The exact paragraph or page relied on
quiz.why: Pin-points let judges find the proposition immediately.

quiz.q: Obiter dicta of the Supreme Court are
options: Persuasive and often given great weight
quiz.why: Courts treat Supreme Court obiter with respect, but they are not strictly binding as ratio.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Drafting the Memorial
courses.summary: Parts of a memorial, statement of jurisdiction, statement of facts, issues, summary of arguments, arguments advanced using IRAC/CRAC, prayer, formatting and an index of authorities, with a worked memorial on the protest-ban problem.

scenes.text: Your memorial has a page limit of 40 pages excluding the cover and index.
Which parts are mandatory?

steps.title: Standard parts
steps.body:
1. Cover page (court, case title, side, team code)
2. Table of contents
3. List of abbreviations
4. Index of authorities (cases, statutes, books, articles, online sources)
5. Statement of jurisdiction
6. Statement of facts
7. Issues raised (questions presented)
8. Summary of arguments
9. Arguments advanced (written pleadings)
10. Prayer

steps.title: Formatting
steps.body: Follow the rules exactly: font (often Times New Roman 12, footnotes 10), line spacing 1.5, margins, colour of cover (often blue for petitioner, red for respondent), team code instead of names. Penalties apply for violations and for exceeding page limits.

steps.title: Consistency
steps.body: Use the same party names and abbreviations throughout; define them once in the abbreviations list.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Revealing team members' names or college in the memorial – this usually leads to disqualification or penalty.

quiz.why: Issues follow facts, then the summary and the detailed arguments.

quiz.why: Anonymity through team codes keeps marking unbiased.

lessons.title: Lab: Statement of jurisdiction and facts

scenes.text: The appellant must show the court has jurisdiction.
The respondent may 'humbly submit' to jurisdiction while reserving objections.

steps.title: Statement of jurisdiction – Appellant
steps.body: 'The Appellant has approached this Hon'ble Court under Article 136 of the Constitution of Indiana, which is pari materia with Article 136 of the Constitution of India, seeking special leave to appeal against the judgment dated 15 March 2026 of the High Court of Mahanagar in W.P. No. 210 of 2026.'

steps.title: Statement of jurisdiction – Respondent
steps.body: 'The Respondent humbly submits to the jurisdiction of this Hon'ble Court under Article 136 of the Constitution of Indiana, while reserving the right to contend that no substantial question of law of general public importance arises warranting interference.'

steps.title: Statement of facts
steps.body: Chronological, neutral-sounding but favourable selection; use headings (Background; The Notification; The Refusal; Proceedings below). No arguments, no facts outside the record, cite paragraph numbers of the moot proposition where allowed.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Copy-pasting the whole moot problem as facts. Summarise and organise them.

quiz.why: Respondents accept the court's jurisdiction while preserving maintainability arguments.

quiz.q: Facts should be

quiz.why: Accuracy to the record is essential to credibility.

scenes.text: Issue 2: whether the ban violates Article 19.
Break it into sub-issues and build each with CRAC.

steps.title: CRAC
steps.body: **Conclusion** (state your answer) → **Rule** (provision + authority) → **Application** (to the facts, with paragraph references) → **Conclusion** (restate). Headings should be argumentative: 'II. THE BLANKET BAN IS A DISPROPORTIONATE RESTRICTION ON ARTICLE 19(1)(a) AND (b).'

steps.title: Worked sub-argument (Appellant)
steps.body:
'2.1 The right to peaceful protest is protected by Article 19(1)(a) and (b).
It is humbly submitted that peaceful assembly without arms is guaranteed. [Rule] Article 19(1)(b); Himat Lal K. Shah (1973) recognised the right to hold public meetings; Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan (2018) held a total ban on protests at a designated site unreasonable. [Application] The Union sought a peaceful, time-bound sit-in of 200 persons (Moot Proposition ¶ 6). [Conclusion] Its activity falls squarely within Article 19(1)(a) and (b).
2.2 The restriction fails proportionality.
[Rule] Restrictions must pursue a legitimate aim, be suitable, necessary (least restrictive) and balanced (Modern Dental College, 2016; Anuradha Bhasin, 2020). [Application] The aim (public order) is legitimate, but an indefinite ban on all gatherings within 2 km, peaceful or not, is not the least restrictive measure; conditions on numbers, timing and policing would suffice. [Conclusion] The ban is disproportionate and void.'

steps.title: Respondent counter
steps.body: 'The violent incident of 3 January (¶ 3) shows a real and proximate threat to public order; Article 19(3) permits restrictions in the interests of public order; Amit Sahni (2020) holds public spaces cannot be occupied indefinitely; an alternative site was offered (¶ 8), showing the restriction is tailored.'

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Long quotations without application. Judges want your reasoning linking the rule to facts.

items: State the conclusion as a heading
State the rule with authority
Apply the rule to specific facts with paragraph references
Address the likely counter-argument
Restate the conclusion

quiz.why: Modern Dental College (2016) and Puttaswamy adopted this four-step test.

quiz.q: Argumentative headings should
quiz.why: Headings in the arguments section state your position, unlike neutral issues.

quiz.q: A good counter for the respondent is
options: Relying on Article 19(3) public order and the alternative site
quiz.why: It ties a constitutional ground to facts in the record.

lessons.title: Lab: Summary of arguments and prayer

scenes.text: Judges often read only the summary before the oral round.
Make it count.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body: One paragraph per issue, mirroring the headings, with no case citations (or only key ones per rules), stating what you will prove and why.

steps.title: Model summary (Issue 2)
steps.body: 'II. The blanket ban violates Article 19. Peaceful protest is protected by Article 19(1)(a) and (b). Although public order is a legitimate aim, an indefinite ban on all gatherings within 2 km, irrespective of size or nature, is not the least restrictive measure available and fails the proportionality test. The offer of a site 12 km away does not cure the defect, as it defeats the communicative purpose of the protest.'

steps.title: Model prayer
Common mistake
steps.body: A prayer that asks for relief not argued, or omits relief that was argued.

items: 'Wherefore' opening referring to issues and arguments
Specific relief 1: set aside judgment
Specific relief 2: declare notification void
Specific relief 3: consequential direction
Residuary prayer for any other order
Signature line: counsel for the party

quiz.why: The reliefs sought must follow from the submissions made.

quiz.why: It gives the bench a quick overview of the case theory.

options: Any other order the court deems fit
quiz.why: It allows the court to mould relief in the interest of justice.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Oral Advocacy and Court Craft
courses.summary: Court etiquette and forms of address, structuring a 15-minute submission, handling judges' questions, time management, rebuttal and sur-rebuttal, and a full oral-round simulation with scripted exchanges.
outcomes: Use correct court etiquette and forms of address
Structure an oral submission with roadmap and signposting
Answer judicial questions directly and return to the roadmap
Deliver a focused two-minute rebuttal

scenes.text: Three judges look up as you rise. Your hands are shaking.
The first 30 seconds decide the judges' impression.

steps.title: Etiquette
steps.body:
- Stand when addressing or being addressed; seek permission to begin.
- Address: 'Your Lordships/Your Ladyships' or 'Hon'ble Court'; many courts now accept 'Your Honour' or 'Sir/Ma'am' (BCI resolution and court notices discourage 'My Lord' in some High Courts).
- Refer to opposing counsel as 'learned counsel for the Respondent'.
- Never interrupt a judge; say 'With respect' or 'I am grateful' when disagreeing or thanking.
- Dress: black coat/blazer, white shirt, bands as per rules.

steps.title: Model opening
steps.body: 'May it please the Court. I am [code], counsel for the Appellant, the Farmers' Union, along with my co-counsel. I shall be addressing Issues 1 and 2, maintainability and the violation of Article 19, in 10 and 5 minutes respectively; my co-counsel will address Issues 3 and 4. With the Court's permission, I seek to reserve 2 minutes for rebuttal. Shall I proceed with a brief summary of facts, or are Your Lordships familiar with them?'

steps.title: Roadmap
steps.body: Tell the bench where you are going: issues, time split, rebuttal reservation.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Reading the memorial aloud. Speak from short notes and maintain eye contact.

items: Seek permission and greet the court
Introduce yourself and co-counsel
State whom you represent
Give the roadmap of issues and time
Reserve time for rebuttal
Offer to summarise facts

quiz.q: Opposing counsel should be referred to as
quiz.why: Courtesy to colleagues is part of court etiquette.

quiz.q: When a judge starts speaking you should
quiz.why: Never interrupt the bench; answering their concern is your priority.

quiz.q: The roadmap tells the bench
options: The issues you will address and time allocation
quiz.why: Signposting helps judges follow and manage time.

scenes.text: Judge: 'Counsel, wasn't the violence on 3 January enough reason for the State to act?'
You have 30 seconds. What do you say?

steps.title: Technique
steps.body:
1. Listen fully; pause.
2. Answer directly – 'Yes', 'No', or 'Yes, but…' – in the first sentence.
3. Give the reason and authority.
4. Link back to your argument and roadmap.
If you don't know: 'I am not aware of that authority, Your Lordship; however, the principle in X suggests…'. Concede weak points that don't hurt your case – it builds credibility.

steps.title: Model answers
steps.body:
Q: 'Wasn't the violence enough reason?'
A: 'Yes, My Lord, the State was entitled to act – but the action must be proportionate. A single incident cannot justify an indefinite ban on all peaceful gatherings; the State could have imposed conditions, as Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan directs. If I may, this takes me to my second sub-issue on necessity.'
Q: 'Isn't the alternative site enough?'
A: 'With respect, no. A protest's purpose is to be seen and heard by the authority addressed; a site 12 km away defeats that purpose, making the restriction excessive.'

steps.title: Hypotheticals
steps.body: Engage hypotheticals; they test the limits of your principle. Distinguish them using a key fact.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Saying 'I will come to that later' to every question. Answer briefly now, then continue.

items: Listen without interrupting
Pause and think
Answer directly in the first sentence
Give the reason and authority
Return to your roadmap

quiz.q: Best first sentence to a yes/no question
options: A direct yes or no (with 'but' if needed)
quiz.why: Judges value directness; elaboration follows.

quiz.q: If you don't know an authority asked about, you should
options: Admit it and argue from principle
quiz.why: Honesty preserves credibility; inventing authority is unethical.

quiz.q: Conceding a minor point
options: Can build credibility if it does not harm the core case
quiz.why: Sensible concessions show judgment and keep focus on stronger points.

scenes.text: The timekeeper holds up '2 minutes'. You still have one sub-issue left.
What do you cut?

steps.title: Managing time
steps.body: Plan your speech in blocks (e.g. 10 minutes: 1 min intro, 4 min sub-issue A, 4 min sub-issue B, 1 min conclusion). Prepare a 'short version' of each point. If time is up: 'I see my time has expired; may I have 30 seconds to conclude?' then give your prayer in one sentence.

steps.title: Rebuttal
steps.body: Only respond to points raised by the opponent – no new arguments. Pick 2–3 strongest points; each in 30–40 seconds: point raised → why it fails → authority/fact. Sur-rebuttal (respondent) answers only rebuttal points.

steps.title: Model rebuttal (2 minutes)
steps.body: 'I am grateful. Three points. First, learned counsel relied on Amit Sahni; but that case concerned indefinite occupation of a public road, whereas the Appellant sought a time-bound sit-in. Second, counsel said the alternative site cures the ban; Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan held that sites must allow meaningful protest. Third, counsel argued the ban is temporary; the notification has no end date (¶ 4). Hence the appeal deserves to be allowed.'

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Raising a new argument in rebuttal. Judges usually disregard it and may penalise.

items.text: Responding to a case cited by the opponent
Introducing a brand-new issue
Correcting a factual misstatement by the opponent
Re-reading your whole argument

quiz.q: Rebuttal must
options: Respond only to the opponent's points
quiz.why: Rebuttal is confined to answering what the other side argued.

quiz.q: When time expires you should
options: Ask for a brief moment to conclude and state the prayer
quiz.why: Respecting time while asking permission to conclude is good practice.

quiz.q: Sur-rebuttal answers
quiz.why: It is limited to points made in the rebuttal.

scenes.text: You are counsel for the Respondent State. The bench is sceptical of the ban.
Defend it with integrity and precision.

steps.title: Respondent's script outline
steps.body:
1. Roadmap: Issue 1 – appeal not maintainable as no substantial question of law; Issue 2 – ban is a reasonable restriction.
2. Facts emphasised: violent protest injuring 14 persons (¶ 3), intelligence inputs of repetition (¶ 5), Secretariat houses emergency services (¶ 2).
3. Law: Article 19(2)–(3) public order; Amit Sahni – public spaces cannot be occupied indefinitely; Ramlila Maidan – State may regulate in the interests of public order but must balance.
4. Concession: 'The Respondent accepts that the ban must be reviewed periodically and is willing to give an undertaking to review it every 30 days.'
5. Prayer: dismiss the appeal.

steps.title: Bench exchange
steps.body:
Judge: 'Why not just limit numbers?'
Counsel: 'My Lady, the intelligence inputs at ¶ 5 indicate that even small gatherings were to be used as a front; the State chose a geographically limited measure while offering an alternative site. However, the Respondent will abide by any direction of this Court to frame a regulated permission scheme.'

steps.title: Self-review
steps.body: Record yourself; check pace (about 130–150 words per minute), filler words, eye contact and whether you answered each question directly.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Defending an indefensible point to the end. A principled concession can save the core argument.

items: Greeting and roadmap
Maintainability objection
Facts supporting public order concern
Law on reasonable restrictions
Strategic concession on periodic review
Prayer

lessons.title: Stages of civil and criminal trials

story.title: First day at the district court

scenes.text: You sit in a courtroom where a judge calls 40 cases in an hour.
To understand what is happening, you need the map of a trial.

steps.title: Civil suit (CPC)
steps.body:
1. Plaint and summons (O. V)
2. Written statement (O. VIII)
3. Admission/denial of documents (O. XI/XII)
4. Framing of issues (O. XIV)
5. ADR referral (s. 89)
6. Plaintiff's evidence: affidavit in chief (O. XVIII R. 4), cross-examination
7. Defendant's evidence
8. Final arguments
9. Judgment (O. XX) and decree
10. Execution (O. XXI)

steps.title: Sessions trial (BNSS)
steps.body:
1. FIR and investigation; police report (chargesheet) under s. 193
2. Cognizance and commitment to Court of Session
3. Opening by prosecutor
4. Discharge (s. 250 – application within 60 days of commitment) or framing of charge (s. 251)
5. Plea of the accused
6. Prosecution evidence (examination-in-chief, cross, re-examination)
7. Statement of accused (s. 351)
8. Arguments on acquittal if no evidence (s. 256)
9. Defence evidence
10. Final arguments; judgment (s. 258); hearing on sentence if convicted.

scenes.text: Your university requires a diary of 10 civil and 10 criminal hearings.
What should each entry contain?

steps.title: Entry format
steps.body: Date; court and presiding officer (designation); case number and title (anonymise parties if required); nature of case and provisions; stage; what happened (arguments, witness examined, order passed); next date; your learning and questions.

steps.title: Sample entry
steps.body: 'Date: 14 July 2026. Court: Additional Sessions Judge-II, Pune. Case: Sessions Case No. 112/2025, State v A.B. Offences: BNS (theft, house-breaking). Stage: prosecution evidence. PW-3 (panch witness) examined-in-chief by APP on the recovery panchnama; cross-examined on discrepancies in time of recovery (10 am in panchnama vs 11 am in deposition). Next date: 28 July 2026 for PW-4. Learning: cross-examination exposed inconsistency without arguing with the witness; judge recorded demeanour note.'

steps.title: Ethics
steps.body: Respect confidentiality; do not record proceedings on phone; seek permission of the presiding officer if needed.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Writing a story without legal analysis. Identify provisions, stage and procedure.

items: Date and court
Case number and title
Nature and provisions
Stage of proceedings
What happened
Next date
Learning and questions

quiz.q: A diary entry should include

steps.title: BSA 2023 rules
steps.body: Order of examination: chief, cross, re-examination (s. 143). **Leading questions** (suggesting the answer) must not be asked in chief or re-examination if objected to, except on introductory/undisputed matters (s. 146); **may** be asked in cross-examination (s. 146(3)). Cross-examination may test veracity, discover who the witness is, and shake credit (s. 148). Previous statements in writing can be used to contradict (s. 148/s. 147 framework; police statements under s. 181 BNSS used only to contradict).

steps.title: Cross-examination plan
steps.body:
Goal: show identification was unreliable.
1. 'You were 40 metres away?' – 'Yes.'
2. 'It was 9 pm in November?' – 'Yes.'
3. 'The streetlight was behind the man you saw?' – 'Yes.'
4. 'You had never seen the accused before?' – 'No.'
5. 'You saw him for a few seconds?' – 'Yes.'
6. 'In your police statement you did not mention the streetlight?' – confront with the statement.
Stop there; argue the inference in final arguments, not with the witness.

steps.title: Golden rules
steps.body: Ask short, leading, one-fact questions; know the answer before you ask; don't ask 'why'; don't ask one question too many.

lessons.title: Lab: Criminal appeal – the chain of circumstances

scenes.text: Moot facts: R was last seen with the deceased V at 10 pm; V's body was found next morning 3 km away; a blood-stained shirt was recovered at R's instance; no eyewitness. Trial court convicted R of murder; High Court confirmed.
You argue the appeal in the Supreme Court of Indiana.

steps.title: Law
steps.body: **Sharad Birdhichand Sarda v State of Maharashtra (1984)** – five golden principles: (1) circumstances must be fully established; (2) consistent only with the hypothesis of guilt; (3) conclusive in nature; (4) exclude every hypothesis except guilt; (5) a complete chain leaving no reasonable ground for innocence. 'Last seen' alone is weak unless the time gap is so small that the possibility of others is ruled out. Recovery statements: only the part distinctly relating to the fact discovered is admissible (s. 23(2) BSA proviso, formerly s. 27 IEA).

steps.title: Arguments
steps.body:
Appellant: time gap of about 10 hours breaks last-seen inference; recovery panch witnesses hostile; no blood-group match reported; motive not proved; chain incomplete (Sarda).
Respondent (State): last seen + recovery + false explanation by accused under s. 351 BNSS form an additional link (Trimukh Maroti Kirkan, 2006, on accused's duty to explain in certain cases); chain complete; concurrent findings should not be disturbed under Article 136 lightly.

steps.title: Bench questions
steps.body: 1. 'Is a false explanation alone enough to convict?' 2. 'What is the time gap and does it matter?' 3. 'Were the recovery witnesses independent?' 4. 'Why should we interfere with concurrent findings?'

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Treating suspicion, however strong, as proof. Suspicion cannot take the place of proof.

scenes.text: Moot facts: SolarCo agreed to supply panels to GridPower by 30 April 2020. A force majeure clause covered 'epidemic, lockdown or government action'. SolarCo's Chinese supplier closed; SolarCo delivered in September 2020. GridPower invoked liquidated damages of 10%.
Arbitral tribunal hearing; you can be either side.

steps.title: Law
steps.body:
- Force majeure is contractual: its scope depends on the clause wording (Energy Watchdog v CERC, 2017 – price rise not force majeure; clause interpreted narrowly).
- Section 32 Contract Act: contracts contingent on events; section 56: frustration where performance becomes impossible or unlawful (Satyabrata Ghose v Mugneeram Bangur, 1954 – 'impossible' includes impracticable in the sense of defeating the object).
- Halliburton Offshore v Vedanta (Delhi HC, 2020): COVID-19 lockdown could not excuse non-performance where the contractor was already in breach before the pandemic.
- Liquidated damages: s. 74 – reasonable compensation not exceeding the named sum; loss need not be proved where hard to quantify, but reasonableness matters (Kailash Nath Associates v DDA, 2015).

steps.title: Arguments
steps.body:
SolarCo: clause expressly covers 'epidemic, lockdown'; causation shown by supplier closure and notice given within the clause period; delay excused; LDs not payable.
GridPower: SolarCo had not placed the order until February 2020 (already late in its schedule); failed to mitigate by alternative sourcing; notice was delayed; force majeure suspends only for the period of the event, not five months after the lockdown eased; LDs reasonable under s. 74.

steps.title: Bench questions
steps.body: 1. 'Was notice given as required by the clause?' 2. 'What steps were taken to mitigate?' 3. 'Was SolarCo already in default before March 2020?' 4. 'Is 10% LD a genuine pre-estimate?'

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Assuming COVID-19 automatically excuses performance. The clause, causation, notice and mitigation must be proved.

Check notice and mitigation requirements

scenes.text: Moot facts: the Union of Indiana enacts a law allowing police to run live facial recognition on CCTV feeds in all public places, retaining data for 10 years, with authorisation by a Superintendent of Police and no judicial oversight.
A civil liberties group files an Article 32 petition.

steps.title: Law
steps.body: **K.S. Puttaswamy v Union of India (2017)**: privacy is a fundamental right under Article 21; any intrusion must satisfy (1) **legality** (a law), (2) **legitimate aim**, (3) **proportionality**, plus procedural safeguards against abuse. Puttaswamy (Aadhaar, 2018) applied it, striking down some provisions (e.g. private use under s. 57). Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023 – exemptions for State instrumentalities on notified grounds (s. 17). PUCL v Union of India (1997) – telephone tapping safeguards.

steps.title: Arguments
steps.body:
Petitioner: law exists (legality satisfied) but blanket, suspicionless surveillance of all public places is not necessary; 10-year retention excessive; no independent/judicial oversight; risk of misidentification and chilling of Article 19 rights – fails proportionality and procedural safeguards.
Union: legitimate aims – national security, crime prevention; public places carry reduced expectation of privacy; SP-level authorisation is a safeguard; technology has proven benefits in finding missing children; data security measures in place.

steps.title: Bench questions
steps.body: 1. 'What less restrictive alternative is available?' 2. 'Is there an expectation of privacy in public?' 3. 'Who audits misuse?' 4. 'Should we read down rather than strike down?'

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Stopping at 'privacy is a fundamental right'. The case turns on proportionality and safeguards.

Remedy: strike down or read down

lessons.title: Nature of the profession and its history

scenes.text: Gandhiji trained as a barrister and wrote that he tried to bring parties together rather than win at any cost.
Why is law called a 'profession' and not a 'business'?

steps.title: Profession vs trade
steps.body: A profession involves specialised learning, a public service element, self-regulation and an ethical code. The advocate is an **officer of the court** with duties to the court, client, opponent, colleagues and society. In Bar Council of Maharashtra v M.V. Dabholkar (1976) the Supreme Court said law is not a trade; touting and advertising degrade it.

steps.title: History
steps.body: Mayor's Courts (1726), Supreme Court at Calcutta (1774) with attorneys and barristers; Legal Practitioners Act 1879 (pleaders, mukhtars, vakils); Indian Bar Councils Act 1926; All India Bar Committee (1951) recommended a unified bar; Law Commission's 14th Report (1958); **Advocates Act 1961** created a single class of 'advocates' and the Bar Council of India.

steps.title: Short note outline
steps.body: 'Legal profession is a noble profession – discuss.' Points: public service, officer of court, monopoly with responsibility (s. 29), duty to assist justice, legal aid (Art. 39A), Dabholkar.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Saying the Advocates Act came in 1951. The Act is of 1961; 1951 is the All India Bar Committee.

steps.title: State Bar Councils (ss. 3, 6)
steps.body: Constituted for each State (or group). Members: Advocate General (ex officio) and elected advocates. Functions (s. 6): admit persons as advocates on its roll, prepare and maintain the roll, **entertain and determine cases of misconduct** against advocates on its roll, safeguard rights and interests of advocates, promote law reform, conduct seminars, organise legal aid, manage funds.

steps.title: Bar Council of India (ss. 4, 7)
steps.body: Members: Attorney General and Solicitor General (ex officio) and one member elected by each State Bar Council. Functions (s. 7): lay down **standards of professional conduct and etiquette**, procedure for disciplinary committees, safeguard rights, promote law reform, deal with matters referred by State Councils, **exercise general supervision and control** over State Councils, promote **legal education** and recognise universities, conduct seminars, organise legal aid, recognise foreign qualifications, manage funds. Appellate disciplinary jurisdiction (s. 37). Rule-making power (s. 49).

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: Client complains to the State Bar Council on whose roll the advocate is enrolled; its disciplinary committee hears under s. 35. She may also file criminal complaint for criminal breach of trust (BNS) separately.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Complaining to the BCI first. Original disciplinary jurisdiction lies with the State Bar Council (BCI can transfer/withdraw under s. 36).

scenes.text: A full-time bank manager with an LLB applies for enrolment as an advocate.
The State Bar Council refuses. Why?

steps.title: Qualifications (s. 24)
steps.body: Citizen of India (foreign nationals on reciprocity), completed **21 years**, law degree from a recognised university, fulfils State Bar Council conditions, pays enrolment fee (s. 24(1)(f) – ₹750 general and ₹125 SC/ST, as held fixed in Gaurav Kumar v Union of India, 2024, which barred higher fees). Must pass the **All India Bar Examination (AIBE)** to get a certificate of practice (upheld in Bar Council of India v Bonnie Foi Law College, 2023, which also allowed final-year students to take it).

steps.title: Disqualifications (s. 24A)
steps.body: Conviction for an offence involving moral turpitude; conviction under the Untouchability (Offences) Act/PCR Act; dismissal or removal from government employment for moral turpitude – disqualification ceases 2 years after release/dismissal. BCI Rules (Part VI, Ch. II, Section VII) restrict advocates from full-time salaried employment or business while practising.

steps.title: Right to practise
steps.body:
- **s. 29**: advocates are the only class of persons entitled to practise law.
- **s. 30**: right to practise throughout India in all courts including the Supreme Court, before tribunals and authorities (brought into force in 2011).
- **s. 32**: court may permit a non-advocate to appear in a particular case.
- **s. 33**: no one other than an enrolled advocate may practise in courts.
- **s. 45**: illegal practice punishable with imprisonment up to 6 months.
**Bar Council of India v A.K. Balaji (2018)**: foreign lawyers cannot practise Indian law; may 'fly in and fly out' for advice on foreign law and in international arbitration. BCI Rules for Registration of Foreign Lawyers (2022) permit limited practice in non-litigious foreign/international law matters.

steps.title: Applying it
steps.body: Bank manager: full-time salaried employment is incompatible with practice (BCI Rules, Rule 49); he may enrol only after leaving employment, or hold enrolment in suspension by declaring non-practice.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Saying a law graduate can appear in court on the strength of the degree alone. Enrolment and the AIBE certificate are needed.

An advocate may be designated senior with consent if the Supreme Court or a High Court is of the opinion that by virtue of ability, standing at the Bar or special knowledge or experience in law, he is deserving of such distinction. Restrictions (BCI Rules, Part VI, Ch. I): a senior advocate shall not file a vakalatnama or act in any court; shall not appear without an advocate-on-record/junior; shall not draft pleadings (may settle them); shall not accept instructions directly from a client.

In 2023 the Court modified it (e.g. removed voting by secret ballot only in exceptional cases, reduced weight on publications). In Jitender @ Kalla v State (NCT of Delhi), 2025, the Court revisited the process and moved away from the points system.

steps.body: Only an Advocate-on-Record may file and act in the Supreme Court (Supreme Court Rules 2013, Order IV): requires training, an examination and an office within 16 km of the Court.

steps.title: Section I (Rules 1–10)
steps.body:
- Act in a dignified, self-respecting manner; submit grievances against a judge to proper authorities (R. 1).
- Maintain respect for the court (R. 2).
- Not influence the decision of a court by illegal or improper means; no private communication with a judge about a pending case (R. 3).
- Use best efforts to restrain the client from unfair practices such as forging documents or bribery; refuse to represent a client who persists (R. 4).
- Appear in prescribed dress, not wear bands/gown in public places except ceremonial occasions (R. 5).
- Not appear before a court where a relative is a member of the bench (R. 6).
- Not appear in matters where he is a pecuniary interest or for an organisation of which he is a member of the executive committee (R. 8–9).
- Not stand as surety for a client (R. 10).

steps.title: Section II (Rules 11–33)
steps.body:
- **R. 11 (cab-rank)**: bound to accept any brief in courts he practises, at a fee consistent with standing, save special circumstances.
- **R. 12**: not withdraw without sufficient cause and reasonable notice; refund unearned fees.
- **R. 13**: not accept a brief where he has reason to believe he will be a witness.
- **R. 14**: full and frank disclosure of connection with parties.
- **R. 15**: fearlessly uphold client's interests by all fair and honourable means.
- **R. 16**: prosecutor shall not suppress material capable of establishing innocence.
- **R. 17**: not disclose client communications (also s. 132 BSA 2023).
- **R. 18**: not foment litigation.
- **R. 20**: no **contingent fee** (share or percentage of the result).
- **R. 21**: not buy or traffic in actionable claims arising from proceedings he is engaged in.
- **R. 22**: not bid for or purchase property sold in proceedings he was engaged in.
- **R. 24**: not adjust fees against personal liability.
- **R. 25–29**: client money accounts (see Unit 5).
- **R. 33**: having advised a party, not appear for the opposite party in the same matter.

steps.body: An advocate took money from elderly clients for filing a suit, never filed it and fabricated stories of progress. steps.title: Section 35 procedure
steps.body:
1. Complaint (or suo motu) to the State Bar Council.
2. If it has 'reason to believe' misconduct occurred, refer to its **disciplinary committee** (s. 35(1)); it may also summarily reject.
3. Committee fixes hearing; notice to the advocate and Advocate General (s. 35(2)).
4. Hearing with opportunity to be heard; committee has civil court powers for summoning and evidence (s. 42).
5. Orders (s. 35(3)): (a) dismiss the complaint (or direct proceedings be filed if initiated suo motu); (b) **reprimand**; (c) **suspend** from practice for such period as it deems fit; (d) **remove** the name from the State roll.
6. If not disposed of within **one year**, proceedings stand transferred to the BCI (s. 36B).

steps.title: Appeals and review
steps.body: Appeal to the BCI within **60 days** (s. 37); further appeal to the **Supreme Court** within **60 days** (s. 38). Review by the disciplinary committee on its own or on application (s. 44). BCI's own disciplinary powers (s. 36) and power to transfer.

steps.title: Worked dates
steps.body: State committee order communicated on 1 March 2026 suspending the advocate for 2 years. Appeal to BCI by 30 April 2026 (60 days). BCI order on 1 October 2026; appeal to SC by 30 November 2026 (60 days).

scenes.text: In 2020 an advocate tweeted criticism of the Supreme Court and the Chief Justice.
The Court held him guilty of criminal contempt and fined him ₹1. Why such a fine?

steps.title: Constitutional basis
steps.body: Article 129 (Supreme Court) and Article 215 (High Courts) – courts of record with power to punish for contempt of themselves. Article 19(2) permits restrictions on speech for contempt of court.

steps.title: Definitions (s. 2)
steps.body:
- **Civil contempt** (s. 2(b)): **wilful disobedience** of any judgment, decree, direction, order, writ or other process of a court, or wilful breach of an undertaking given to a court.
- **Criminal contempt** (s. 2(c)): publication (by words, signs, visible representations) or doing any act which (i) **scandalises** or tends to scandalise, or lowers or tends to lower the authority of any court; (ii) prejudices or interferes with the due course of any judicial proceeding; or (iii) interferes with or obstructs the administration of justice.

steps.title: Defences and limits
steps.body:
- Innocent publication and distribution (s. 3).
- Fair and accurate report of judicial proceedings (s. 4).
- **Fair criticism** of a judicial act after the case is heard and finally decided (s. 5).
- Complaint against presiding officers of subordinate courts made in good faith (s. 6).
- **Truth** as a valid defence if in public interest and bona fide (s. 13(b), 2006).
- No punishment unless the contempt substantially interferes or tends to interfere with due course of justice (s. 13(a)).
- **Punishment** (s. 12): simple imprisonment up to **six months**, or fine up to **₹2,000**, or both; apology may remit; for civil contempt, court may detain in civil prison instead of fine.
- **Limitation** (s. 20): no proceedings after **one year** from the date of the alleged contempt.
- Criminal contempt of subordinate courts is referred by them to the High Court; Advocate General's consent needed for others to move (s. 15).

steps.title: In re Prashant Bhushan (2020)
steps.body: Held guilty of criminal contempt for two tweets; fined ₹1, in default 3 months' simple imprisonment and 3 years' debarment from practice. In In re Vinay Chandra Mishra (1995), a senior advocate who shouted at a High Court judge was convicted and given a suspended sentence.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Thinking any criticism of a judgment is contempt. Fair, reasoned criticism after a decision is protected (s. 5).

steps.title: Mutual respect
steps.body: The bar and bench are two wheels of the chariot of justice. Advocate's duties: respect the court (R. 1–2), not use intemperate language, assist the court honestly, cite adverse precedents. Judges: patience, courtesy, not humiliate counsel, decide without bias, hear both sides. Grievances against judges go to the Chief Justice or administrative side, not to the press or by disrupting court.

steps.title: Guidance
steps.body: Restatement of Values of Judicial Life (1997) adopted by the Supreme Court; Bangalore Principles of Judicial Conduct (2002): independence, impartiality, integrity, propriety, equality, competence. Strikes and boycotts – illegal (Harish Uppal, 2003; District Bar Association Dehradun v Ishwar Shandilya, 2020).

steps.title: Applying it
steps.body: Counsel should respond calmly, request time if needed, and later submit a respectful representation to the Chief Justice if conduct was improper. Answering back in anger can be contempt (Vinay Chandra Mishra).

steps.body: Believing strikes are a legitimate protest tool for advocates. The Supreme Court has repeatedly held them illegal.

steps.title: BCI Rules 25–29 and books
steps.body:
- R. 25: money received from or on behalf of a client must be kept in a separate account.
- R. 26: where money is received for a specific purpose, it is to be used for that purpose only; balance refunded.
- R. 27: money received on behalf of a client shall be informed to the client and paid within a reasonable time (unless he has a lien for agreed fees).
- R. 28: on termination, adjust fees and refund balance.
- R. 29: copy of account to be furnished on demand.
Books typically maintained: **cash book**, **bank book** (office and client accounts), **client ledger** (one per client), **diary** of cases and fees, receipt book. Accounting principle: double entry; client money is a liability, not income.

steps.title: Constitutional and statutory basis
steps.body: Article 39A (42nd Amendment) – equal justice and free legal aid. Article 21 – right to free legal aid at State cost for an accused who cannot afford a lawyer (Hussainara Khatoon, 1979; M.H. Hoskot v State of Maharashtra, 1978; Khatri v State of Bihar, 1981 – duty arises from first production before a magistrate). Legal Services Authorities Act 1987: NALSA, SLSAs, DLSAs, Taluk committees; legal aid clinics; para-legal volunteers; Legal Aid Defence Counsel System (2022).

steps.title: Section 12 – entitlement
steps.body: Members of Scheduled Castes or Tribes; victims of trafficking or begar; women and children; persons with disabilities; victims of mass disaster, ethnic violence, caste atrocity, flood, drought, earthquake or industrial disaster; industrial workmen; persons in custody (including protective homes, juvenile homes, psychiatric hospitals); persons with annual income below the limit notified by the State (or ₹5 lakh for Supreme Court cases under the SCLSC regulations, as revised).

steps.title: Applying it
steps.body: A woman seeking maintenance is entitled to free legal services regardless of income (s. 12(c)). She applies to the DLSA, which assigns a panel lawyer; court fees and expenses are borne by the authority.

steps.title: Privilege under the BSA 2023
steps.body: Section 132 (formerly s. 126 Evidence Act): an advocate shall not disclose communications made by the client in the course of employment, nor contents of documents, nor advice given, without express consent. Exceptions: communication in furtherance of an illegal purpose; any fact observed showing crime or fraud committed since employment began. The privilege continues after employment ends. Section 134: no one can be compelled to disclose confidential communication with legal adviser. In 2025 the Supreme Court restrained investigating agencies from summoning advocates merely for advice given to clients (suo motu case on summons to advocates), subject to exceptions under s. 132.

steps.title: Conflicts
steps.body: Rule 33: not appear for the opposite party in the same matter after advising one side. Rule 14: disclose any interest or connection. Joint representation of co-accused is permissible only where defences do not conflict; once conflict arises, the advocate must withdraw from at least one, and may need to withdraw from both if confidences from one would be relevant to the other. Firms: conflicts of one partner are generally imputed to the firm.

steps.title: Applying it
steps.body: Co-accused conflict: the advocate cannot cross-examine the approver (former client) using confidential information; should withdraw from representing the approver and possibly both; inform the court so the accused is not left unrepresented (legal aid can be arranged).

steps.body: Thinking privilege ends when the case ends. It continues even after employment ceases.

uni-llb-property-law.title: Property Law: Transfer of Property Act & Easements
uni-llb-property-law.description: General principles of transfer, sale, mortgage and charge, lease, gift, exchange and actionable claims under the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, and easements and licences under the Indian Easements Act, 1882. General education, not legal advice. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian LLB programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · General principles of transfer (TPA ss. 5–37)
courses.summary: What a 'transfer of property' is, what can and cannot be transferred, conditions restraining alienation, transfers to unborn persons, the rule against perpetuity, vested and contingent interests, and conditional transfers.
outcomes: Define transfer of property under section 5 and distinguish it from partition, surrender and release
Identify property that cannot be transferred under section 6
Apply sections 10 to 12 on conditions restraining alienation and enjoyment

lessons.title: Meaning of transfer and transferable property (ss. 5–6)

story.title: The farmer and the future crop

scenes.text: Ramesh wants to sell his hope of inheriting his uncle's land, and also his right to sue a neighbour for damages for trespass.
A buyer offers money for both. His lawyer says neither can legally be sold. Why?

steps.title: Section 5: transfer defined
steps.body:
A **transfer of property** is an act by which a **living person** conveys property, in present or in future, to one or more other living persons, or to himself and others. 'Living person' includes a company, association or body of individuals, whether incorporated or not.

Key features: (1) act inter vivos (wills are excluded); (2) conveyance of an existing interest; (3) present or future operation; (4) between living persons.

steps.title: Section 6: what cannot be transferred
steps.body:
Property of any kind may be transferred, except, among others:
- (a) **spes successionis** – the chance of an heir apparent succeeding, or of a relation obtaining a legacy
- (b) a mere **right of re-entry** for breach of condition, except to the owner of the property affected
- (c) an **easement** apart from the dominant heritage
- (d) an interest restricted in enjoyment to the owner personally
- (dd) a right to future **maintenance**
- (e) a **mere right to sue**
- (f) a **public office** or salary of a public officer
- (g) stipends and pensions of government military/civil pensioners
- (h) transfers opposed to the nature of the interest, for an unlawful object, or to a legally disqualified transferee
- (i) certain non-transferable occupancy interests

steps.title: Applying s.6 to Ramesh
steps.body:
1. Hope of inheriting the uncle's land = spes successionis → s.6(a) bars transfer; even a deed and payment cannot make it valid, though money paid may be recoverable.
2. Right to sue for trespass damages = mere right to sue → s.6(e) bars transfer.
3. By contrast, a debt already due (an actionable claim) **can** be transferred under ss.130 onwards.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating a will as a 'transfer' under s.5 – it operates after death and is governed by succession law.
- Confusing a mere right to sue (not transferable) with an actionable claim such as a book debt (transferable).
- Forgetting that a partition among co-owners is generally not a transfer of new title but a division of existing title.

steps.title: Immovable property
steps.body: Section 3 says immovable property does not include standing timber, growing crops or grass. The General Clauses Act, 1897 adds that it includes land, benefits arising out of land, and things attached to the earth.

activity.prompt: Tick every item that CANNOT be transferred under section 6
items: The chance of an heir apparent to succeed to an estate
A mere right to sue for damages
A right to future maintenance
A salary of a public officer
An easement detached from the dominant heritage

quiz.q: Which of these is transferable under the TPA?
quiz.why: A book debt is an actionable claim, which sections 130 onwards expressly allow to be transferred by written instrument.

quiz.q: 'Living person' in section 5 includes
quiz.why: Section 5 expressly says living person includes a company or association or body of individuals, incorporated or not.

quiz.q: A transfer by will is
options: Outside the TPA because it is not inter vivos
quiz.why: The TPA deals with transfers between living persons, so testamentary dispositions are governed by succession law instead.

scenes.text: A father gifts a house to his son on condition that the son shall never sell or mortgage it.
Ten years later the son sells it. The father's other children say the sale breaches the condition.

steps.title: Section 10: absolute restraint is void
steps.body: Where property is transferred subject to a condition **absolutely restraining** the transferee from parting with or disposing of his interest, the **condition is void** and the transfer stands. Exceptions: (1) a lease where the condition is for the benefit of the lessor; (2) property transferred to or for a woman (not a Hindu, Muslim or Buddhist) so that she has no power during marriage to transfer it.

steps.title: Absolute vs partial restraint
steps.body:
- **Absolute**: 'shall never sell to anyone' → void.
- **Partial**: 'shall not sell outside the family' – courts examine whether it, in substance, takes away the power of alienation. A restriction that leaves a genuine and real field of alienation may be upheld; one that leaves only an illusory field is treated as absolute.

**Section 11**: where an absolute interest is created, a direction restricting the manner of enjoyment is disregarded (e.g., a house given absolutely 'to be used only as a residence by the donee' – the direction is void as against the transferee).

**Section 12**: a condition that the interest shall cease on insolvency or on attempted alienation is void (except in favour of the transferor himself in certain settlements).

steps.title: Solving the 'never sell' gift
steps.body:
1. Identify: gift creates absolute interest in the son.
2. Condition: never sell or mortgage = absolute restraint.
3. Apply s.10: condition void; gift valid.
4. Result: the son's sale is valid; the siblings have no claim based on the condition.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the whole transfer is void – only the condition fails.
- Forgetting the lease exception: a covenant in a lease not to sublet without consent is valid.

steps.title: Exam answer structure
steps.body: Rule → exceptions → absolute vs partial test → apply to facts → conclusion on both the condition and the transfer.

activity.prompt: Order the steps to analyse a condition attached to a transfer
items: Identify the interest created (absolute or limited)
Read the condition and classify it as restraint on alienation or on enjoyment
Decide whether the restraint is absolute or partial in substance
Check the statutory exceptions (lease, certain women's property)
State whether the condition is void and whether the transfer survives

quiz.q: Under s.10 an absolute restraint on alienation
options: Converts the transfer to a lease
quiz.why: Section 10 strikes down the condition while leaving the transfer itself operative.

quiz.q: A lease covenant forbidding sub-letting for the lessor's benefit is
quiz.why: Section 10 expressly saves conditions in a lease that are for the benefit of the lessor or those claiming under him.

quiz.q: A condition that the donee's interest ends if he becomes insolvent is generally
quiz.why: Section 12 makes void conditions making an interest determinable on insolvency or attempted alienation.

lessons.title: Transfer to unborn persons and the rule against perpetuity (ss. 13–14)

scenes.text: Ali transfers land to his son for life, and then to the son's first child to be born, absolutely.
A second deed gives land to the son for life, then to his unborn child for life, then to that child's children. Which deed works?

steps.title: Section 13
steps.body: Property cannot be transferred **directly** to an unborn person. It can be done only by creating a **prior interest** in a living person, and the interest to the unborn person must extend to the **whole remaining interest** of the transferor. So a life estate to an unborn person is not allowed.

steps.title: Section 14: rule against perpetuity
steps.body:
No transfer can create an interest that is to take effect after the lifetime of one or more persons living at the date of transfer **and** the minority of some person who shall be in existence at the expiry of that period. The maximum remoteness = life(s) in being + minority of the ultimate beneficiary (+ gestation where applicable).

Section 18 exempts transfers for the benefit of the public (religion, knowledge, commerce, health, safety).

steps.title: Solving the two deeds
steps.body:
Deed 1: son (living) gets life interest; first child (unborn) gets the whole remaining interest absolutely → valid under s.13; vesting happens at the latest on the son's death, within s.14.

Deed 2: unborn child gets only a life interest → fails s.13 because it is not the whole remaining interest; the gift to the grandchildren also fails (s.16: an interest that depends on a failed prior interest fails).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying the English 21-year period: in India the extension is the minority of the beneficiary.
- Forgetting that s.13 and s.14 must both be satisfied.
- Missing s.16: ulterior gifts dependent on a failed prior interest also fail.

steps.title: Section 20
steps.body: An unborn person acquires a vested interest on birth, unless the terms of transfer show otherwise, even though he may not be entitled to enjoy it immediately.

activity.prompt: Tick the requirements for a valid transfer benefiting an unborn person
items: A prior interest is created in favour of a living person
The unborn person takes the whole remaining interest of the transferor
The interest vests within the perpetuity period of s.14
The unborn person is in existence before the prior interest ends

quiz.q: Under s.13 an unborn person may receive
options: The whole remaining interest after a prior interest
quiz.why: Section 13 allows benefit to an unborn person only through a prior interest and only of the whole remaining interest.

quiz.q: Indian perpetuity period is life in being plus
quiz.why: Section 14 extends the period by the minority of a person in existence when the lives in being expire.

quiz.q: Transfers for the benefit of the public are
options: Exempt from the perpetuity rule under s.18
quiz.why: Section 18 exempts transfers for the public benefit, such as advancement of religion, knowledge or health, from the restrictions of sections 14 to 16.

lessons.title: Vested, contingent and conditional transfers; election (ss. 19–35)

scenes.text: Meera's grandmother transfers a flat 'to Meera when she attains 25 years'. Meera is 19 and dies at 22.
Does the flat pass to Meera's heirs or go back to the grandmother?

steps.title: Vested interest (s.19)
steps.body: An interest is **vested** when it is created in favour of a person without specifying the time when it is to take effect, or with words that it shall take effect immediately, or on the happening of an event that must happen. Vesting is not defeated by the transferee's death before possession; it passes to his heirs.

steps.title: Contingent interest (s.21)
steps.body:
An interest is **contingent** when it is to take effect only on the happening of a specified **uncertain** event, or if a specified uncertain event shall not happen. It becomes vested when the event happens. If the transferee dies before the event, the interest fails.

The explanation to s.21: a gift to A on attaining a certain age, where the income is given to A meanwhile, is vested, not contingent.

steps.title: Solving Meera's case
steps.body:
1. Event: attaining 25 – uncertain, because she may die earlier.
2. No intermediate enjoyment given to her.
3. Interest is contingent (s.21).
4. She died at 22: the event never happened, so the interest fails and the flat stays with the grandmother (or her estate).
If the deed had said 'income to Meera until 25, then the flat', it would be vested and pass to Meera's heirs.

steps.title: Other rules
steps.body:
- **Condition precedent** (s.25): impossible, immoral or unlawful conditions make the transfer void.
- **Substantial compliance** (s.26) suffices for a condition precedent.
- **Condition subsequent** (s.31-32) must be valid; strict compliance is required.
- **Election** (s.35): one who takes a benefit under an instrument must also accept its burden; he cannot approbate and reprobate.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Calling every postponed enjoyment contingent. Ask: is the event certain (vested) or uncertain (contingent)? Is intermediate income given?

activity.prompt: Order the test for vested vs contingent
items: Identify the event on which the interest depends
Ask whether the event is certain or uncertain
Check whether intermediate enjoyment is given to the transferee
Classify the interest as vested or contingent
Decide what happens if the transferee dies before the event

quiz.q: A gift 'to A on the death of B' is
quiz.why: Death of B is certain to happen, so under s.19 the interest is vested though enjoyment is postponed.

quiz.q: A contingent interest becomes vested
options: When the specified uncertain event happens
quiz.why: Section 21 states the contingent interest becomes vested on the happening of the event.

quiz.q: The doctrine that a person cannot accept the benefit and reject the burden of the same instrument is
quiz.why: Election under section 35 forces a person to choose between conforming to the instrument or dissenting from it.

questions.why: Section 5 defines transfer as an act by which a living person conveys property to other living persons.

options: A mere chance of succession and not transferable
questions.why: Section 6(a) bars transfer of the chance of an heir apparent succeeding to an estate.
Section 6(dd) specifically excludes a right to future maintenance however arising.

questions.why: Section 3 expressly states immovable property does not include standing timber, growing crops or grass.

questions.q: A gift with condition 'never to sell' results in
questions.why: Section 10 voids the absolute restraint but keeps the transfer operative.

questions.q: Which restraint is saved by s.10?
options: Condition in a lease for the lessor's benefit
questions.why: The lease exception allows a lessor to restrain assignment or subletting for his own benefit.

questions.q: A transfer 'to my son for life, then to his unborn daughter for life' — the daughter's interest
questions.why: Section 13 requires the unborn person to take the whole remaining interest, so a life interest fails.

questions.q: Section 18 exempts from the perpetuity rule transfers for
questions.why: Section 18 exempts transfers for the benefit of the public such as advancement of religion, knowledge, health or commerce.

questions.q: An interest dependent on an uncertain event is
questions.why: Section 21 defines a contingent interest by reference to an uncertain event.

questions.q: A gift to A at 21 with income to A meanwhile is
options: Vested by the explanation to s.21
questions.why: Where intermediate income is given, the law treats the interest as vested despite the age condition.

questions.q: A condition precedent that is impossible
options: Makes the transfer fail under s.25
questions.why: Section 25 says an interest on a condition that is impossible, illegal or immoral cannot take effect.

questions.q: Doctrine of election is in section
questions.why: Section 35 codifies election — no one may take a benefit and repudiate the burden of the same instrument.

questions.q: A mere right to sue is non-transferable under
questions.why: Section 6(e) bars transfer of a mere right to sue, to discourage trafficking in litigation.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Key doctrines: ostensible owner, estoppel, lis pendens, fraudulent transfer, part performance
courses.summary: The protective doctrines of the TPA: transfer by ostensible owner (s.41), feeding the grant by estoppel (s.43), lis pendens (s.52), fraudulent transfer (s.53) and part performance (s.53A), with notice under s.3.
outcomes: Apply the conditions of s.41 to protect a bona fide transferee
Explain feeding the grant by estoppel under s.43
Apply lis pendens to transfers during pending litigation
Distinguish s.53 fraudulent transfers from genuine ones
State and apply the six conditions of part performance under s.53A

scenes.text: Sunita bought a flat in her brother Vikram's name and let him live there and hold the papers for years.
Vikram sells the flat to Neha, who checked the registry and paid full price. Sunita sues to cancel the sale.

steps.title: Rule in s.41
steps.body: Where, with the **consent, express or implied**, of the real owner, a person is the **ostensible owner** of immovable property and transfers it for **consideration**, the transfer is not voidable on the ground that the transferor was not authorised, provided the transferee, after taking **reasonable care** to ascertain that the transferor had power to transfer, acted in **good faith**.

steps.title: Applying to Neha
steps.body:
1. Vikram was ostensible owner – title in his name.
2. Sunita consented by keeping it in his name.
3. Sale was for consideration.
4. Neha took reasonable care (registry search) and acted in good faith.
Result: s.41 protects Neha; Sunita's remedy lies against Vikram. (Note: the Prohibition of Benami Property Transactions Act, 1988 may separately affect Sunita's claim.)

steps.title: Notice under s.3
steps.body: A person has notice of a fact when he **actually knows** it, or but for **wilful abstention** from inquiry or **gross negligence** he would have known it (constructive notice). Registration of a required instrument and actual possession of a person are deemed notice in specified cases; notice to an agent is notice to the principal.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- s.41 does not apply to gifts (no consideration).
- The real owner's consent is essential; a forger is not an ostensible owner.
- Skipping the 'reasonable care' element – the burden is on the transferee.

activity.prompt: Tick each element a transferee must prove to claim s.41 protection
items: Transferor was ostensible owner
Real owner consented expressly or impliedly
Transfer was for consideration
Transferee took reasonable care to check title
Transferee acted in good faith

quiz.q: s.41 protects a transferee who takes
options: A transfer for consideration in good faith
quiz.why: The section requires consideration and good faith after reasonable inquiry, so gratuitous transferees are excluded.

quiz.q: Constructive notice arises from
options: Wilful abstention from inquiry or gross negligence
quiz.why: Section 3 imputes knowledge where the person would have known the fact but for wilful abstention or gross negligence.

quiz.q: Whose consent is needed for ostensible ownership?
quiz.why: The doctrine rests on estoppel against a real owner who allowed another to appear as owner.

scenes.text: Karan, falsely claiming to own his father's shop, sells it to Imran for money.
Later the father dies and Karan inherits the shop. Can Imran claim it?

steps.title: Rule
steps.body: Where a person **fraudulently or erroneously represents** that he is authorised to transfer immovable property and professes to transfer it for consideration, the transfer shall, **at the option of the transferee**, operate on any interest the transferor may later acquire, as long as the contract subsists. A later bona fide transferee for consideration without notice of the option is protected.

steps.title: Solving Karan's case
steps.body:
1. Erroneous/fraudulent representation of authority – yes.
2. Transfer for consideration – yes.
3. Karan later acquired the interest by inheritance.
4. Imran may elect to take the shop; the acquired title 'feeds' the earlier grant.
If Karan had sold the shop again to a buyer in good faith without notice, that buyer would prevail.

steps.title: Contrast with s.6(a)
steps.body: s.6(a) bars transfer of a mere expectancy. s.43 applies where the transferor misrepresented present title. Courts have held s.43 can apply where an heir represented that he was owner, since the transferee was misled (see Jumma Masjid, Mercara v Kodimaniandra Deviah, SC 1962).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- s.43 gives an **option** to the transferee, not an automatic transfer.
- It does not defeat a later bona fide purchaser without notice.

items: Find a representation of authority to transfer
Confirm the transfer was for consideration
Show the transferor later acquired the interest
Check the contract still subsists
Check for any later bona fide purchaser without notice
Transferee exercises the option to claim the interest

quiz.q: Under s.43 the later-acquired interest passes
options: At the option of the transferee
quiz.why: Section 43 makes the transfer operate on the later interest only if the transferee so chooses.

quiz.q: Which case is linked with s.43 and an expectant heir?
quiz.why: In Jumma Masjid the Supreme Court applied s.43 where an heir had represented present title.

quiz.q: s.43 does not affect
options: A later bona fide transferee for consideration without notice
quiz.why: The proviso protects good-faith purchasers for value without notice of the earlier option.

scenes.text: Anil sues Bhaskar claiming title to a plot. While the suit is pending, Bhaskar sells the plot to Chetan.
Anil wins. Chetan says he bought in good faith.

steps.title: Lis pendens (s.52)
steps.body: During the pendency of a suit or proceeding (not collusive) in which **any right to immovable property is directly and specifically in question**, the property cannot be transferred by any party so as to affect the rights of any other party under the eventual decree, except under the court's authority. Pendency begins on presentation of the plaint and continues until final disposal including execution. Good faith of the buyer is irrelevant.

steps.title: Applying to Chetan
steps.body:
1. Suit about title to the plot – right directly in question.
2. Transfer by a party (Bhaskar) during pendency.
3. Not authorised by the court.
Result: the sale is not void, but it is subject to the decree; Chetan is bound by Anil's decree. His remedy is against Bhaskar.

steps.title: Fraudulent transfer (s.53)
steps.body: A transfer of immovable property made with **intent to defeat or delay creditors** is voidable at the option of any creditor so defeated or delayed. Rights of a transferee in good faith and for consideration are protected. A suit to avoid it is brought on behalf of all creditors. A gratuitous transfer with intent to defraud a subsequent transferee is voidable at that transferee's option (s.53(2)).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying lis pendens makes the transfer void – it only makes it subject to the result.
- Applying s.52 where the property is not directly in issue (e.g., a money suit).

activity.prompt: Tick the conditions for lis pendens
items: A suit or proceeding is pending in a competent court
The suit is not collusive
A right to immovable property is directly and specifically in question
A party transfers the property during pendency
The transfer is not authorised by the court

quiz.q: A transfer hit by lis pendens is
options: Subject to the decree in the suit
quiz.why: Section 52 binds the transferee by the result of the litigation without declaring the transfer void.

quiz.q: Does a buyer's good faith avoid s.52?
quiz.why: Lis pendens rests on public policy that litigation must be effective, so notice and good faith are irrelevant.

quiz.q: s.53 transfers are voidable at the option of
quiz.why: Section 53 lets defrauded creditors avoid transfers made to defeat or delay them.

scenes.text: Farida signs a written agreement to sell her house to Gopal for ₹40 lakh, takes ₹35 lakh and hands over possession.
Before executing the sale deed she tries to evict Gopal, saying he has no title.

steps.title: The six conditions
steps.body:
1. A **contract** to transfer immovable property for consideration.
2. Made **in writing**, signed by or on behalf of the transferor.
3. Terms can be ascertained with reasonable certainty.
4. Transferee has **taken possession** (or, if already in possession, continues in part performance).
5. Transferee has **done some act in furtherance** of the contract.
6. Transferee has **performed or is willing to perform** his part.
Then the transferor cannot enforce any right against the transferee in respect of the property other than one expressly provided by the contract.

steps.title: Applying to Gopal
steps.body: Written agreement signed by Farida ✔; terms certain ✔; possession taken ✔; ₹35 lakh paid ✔; Gopal ready to pay the balance ₹5 lakh ✔. So Farida cannot evict him. s.53A is a **shield, not a sword**: Gopal defends possession but does not get title; he must sue for specific performance to obtain a sale deed.

steps.title: 2001 amendment
steps.body: After the 2001 amendments to the TPA and Registration Act, a contract for s.53A must be **registered** to claim its benefit, and the words that it is not necessary to register were removed.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Claiming s.53A confers ownership – it does not.
- Relying on an oral agreement – writing is mandatory.
- Ignoring willingness to perform: a defaulting buyer loses protection.

activity.prompt: Order the facts a defendant pleads to invoke s.53A

Terms ascertainable with reasonable certainty
Possession taken in part performance
Act done in furtherance of the contract
Readiness and willingness to perform the remaining part
Transferor barred from enforcing rights against possession

quiz.why: Courts describe s.53A as defensive: it protects possession but does not create a cause of action for title.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a requirement of s.53A?
quiz.why: Full payment is not required; the transferee need only have performed or be willing to perform his part.

quiz.q: After 2001, to claim s.53A the contract must be
quiz.why: The 2001 amendment requires registration of such contracts for s.53A protection.

questions.why: Ostensible ownership must exist with the express or implied consent of the real owner.
Section 3 recognises actual knowledge and imputed knowledge from wilful abstention or gross negligence.

questions.why: Section 43 lets a later-acquired interest feed an earlier unauthorised transfer.
The transferee chooses whether to take the later-acquired interest.

options: A right to immovable property is directly in question

questions.why: The section applies only to written contracts signed by or on behalf of the transferor.
Part performance protects possession against the transferor but does not transfer ownership.

lessons.title: Sale: definition, mode and rights of parties (ss. 54–55)

scenes.text: Deepak pays ₹25 lakh for a plot and gets a signed but unregistered 'sale deed' on stamp paper.
The seller then sells the same plot by registered deed to another buyer. Who owns it?

steps.title: Section 54
steps.body:
**Sale** is a transfer of ownership in exchange for a price paid or promised or part-paid and part-promised.

Mode: tangible immovable property of value ₹100 or more, and a reversion or other intangible thing, can be sold only by a **registered instrument**. Below ₹100, by registered instrument or by delivery of the property.

A **contract for sale** is a contract that a sale shall take place on agreed terms; it **does not by itself create any interest or charge** on the property.

steps.title: Solving Deepak's case
steps.body:
1. Plot worth far over ₹100 → registration compulsory.
2. Deepak's deed is unregistered → no ownership passes; at best it evidences a contract for sale.
3. The second buyer's registered deed transfers ownership.
4. Deepak may sue the seller for refund/damages, or specific performance if facts allow (subject to the second buyer's notice).
See also Suraj Lamp & Industries v State of Haryana (SC 2011): GPA/agreement-to-sell 'sales' do not convey title.

steps.title: Section 55 highlights
steps.body:
Seller must: disclose material latent defects; produce title documents for examination; answer relevant questions on title; execute a proper conveyance; take reasonable care of property till delivery; give possession; pay outgoings till sale. Seller is deemed to warrant that the interest subsists and he has power to transfer.
Buyer must: disclose facts increasing value known to him but not the seller; pay the price; bear loss after ownership passes; pay outgoings after sale. Unpaid seller has a **charge** for unpaid price.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking an agreement to sell transfers ownership.
- Thinking possession alone transfers title of property above ₹100.
- Forgetting the unpaid seller's charge under s.55(4)(b).

activity.prompt: Tick the duties of a seller before completion under s.55
items: Disclose material latent defects
