story.title: Six ways to borrow on land

scenes.text: A bank officer explains to farmers that a loan secured on land can be structured in six different ways.
Each type changes who holds possession, who gets rents, and how the lender recovers.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body: A **mortgage** is the transfer of an **interest in specific immovable property** for the purpose of securing the payment of money advanced or to be advanced by way of loan, an existing or future debt, or performance of an engagement giving rise to pecuniary liability. Parties: mortgagor and mortgagee; principal + interest = mortgage-money; instrument = mortgage-deed.

steps.title: The six kinds
steps.body:
1. **Simple mortgage** – no possession; mortgagor personally binds himself to pay; on default mortgagee may get the property sold through court.
2. **Mortgage by conditional sale** – ostensible sale with condition that on default the sale becomes absolute, or on payment it becomes void/reconveyed; condition must be in the **same document**.
3. **Usufructuary mortgage** – possession delivered; mortgagee takes rents and profits in lieu of interest/principal; no personal liability.
4. **English mortgage** – absolute transfer with covenant to retransfer on repayment; personal liability.
5. **Mortgage by deposit of title deeds** (equitable) – delivery of title documents with intent to create security, in notified towns (Kolkata, Chennai, Mumbai and others notified).
6. **Anomalous mortgage** – any other combination.

steps.title: Classify these
steps.body:
- 'I sell the field to X; if I repay ₹2 lakh in 3 years, X shall reconvey' in the same deed → conditional sale.
- 'X shall be in possession and take crops until the loan is repaid' → usufructuary.
- Customer hands title deeds to a bank in Mumbai for an overdraft → deposit of title deeds.
- 'I bind myself to pay; property may be sold if I fail', no possession → simple.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating a sale with a repurchase option in a separate document as a mortgage by conditional sale – the condition must be in the same document.
- Forgetting that a usufructuary mortgagee has no personal remedy against the mortgagor.

quiz.why: A usufructuary mortgagee takes possession and appropriates rents and profits.

quiz.why: The proviso to s.58(c) says no transaction is a mortgage by conditional sale unless the condition is in the document effecting the sale.

lessons.title: Redemption, clog on redemption and mortgagee's remedies

scenes.text: A mortgage deed says the mortgagor may redeem only after 99 years, and if not repaid within 5 years the property becomes the lender's forever.
The borrower tenders the full loan in year 3.

steps.title: Right of redemption (s.60)
steps.body: At any time after the principal money has become due, the mortgagor has a right, on payment or tender of the mortgage-money at a proper time and place, to require the mortgagee to return the deed and documents, deliver possession if in possession, and retransfer the property. The right is extinguished only by act of parties or decree of court. Maxim: **once a mortgage, always a mortgage**.

steps.title: Clog on redemption
steps.body: Any condition that prevents or unreasonably postpones redemption, or converts the mortgage into a sale on default, is a **clog** and is void. Courts may allow reasonable terms but strike oppressive ones (see Seth Ganga Dhar v Shankar Lal, SC 1958: 'redemption only after 85 years' clause examined as a clog).

steps.title: Mortgagee's rights
steps.body:
- **Foreclosure or sale** (s.67) – suit for decree debarring redemption or for sale.
- **Sue for mortgage-money** (s.68) in specified cases.
- **Power of sale without court** (s.69) – mainly in English mortgages and where permitted.
- Banks also use the SARFAESI Act, 2002 for secured assets.
Related doctrines: **marshalling** (s.81), **contribution** (s.82), **subrogation** (s.92).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating the right of redemption as a mere contractual right; it is statutory and equitable.
- Confusing marshalling (subsequent purchaser) with contribution (co-owners sharing the debt).

quiz.why: The maxim means a mortgage cannot be turned into something that destroys the mortgagor's right to redeem.

quiz.q: The right of redemption is in section
quiz.why: Section 60 states the mortgagor's right to redeem after the principal becomes due.

quiz.q: A clause making the property absolutely the mortgagee's on default is
quiz.why: Converting a mortgage into an absolute transfer on default clogs the equity of redemption and is void.

scenes.text: A family court decree makes a wife's maintenance a charge on her husband's farmland.
The husband sells the farm. Can the wife still recover from it?

steps.title: Charge defined
steps.body: Where immovable property of one person is, by **act of parties or operation of law**, made security for payment of money to another, and the transaction does not amount to a mortgage, the latter has a **charge** on the property. Examples: unpaid seller's charge (s.55(4)(b)), buyer's charge for prepaid price (s.55(6)(b)), maintenance charges by decree.

steps.title: Mortgage vs charge
steps.body:
| Point | Mortgage | Charge |
|---|---|---|
| Nature | Transfer of interest | No transfer, only a right of payment out of property |
| Creation | Act of parties | Act of parties or operation of law |
| Against transferee | Enforceable against all | Not enforceable against a transferee for value without notice (s.100) |
| Limitation | 12 years for mortgage-money suit; 30 for redemption | 12 years |
| Personal remedy | Often available | Generally not, unless agreed |

steps.title: The wife's maintenance
steps.body:
1. Decree created a charge by operation of law.
2. Buyer of the farm: if he bought for value **without notice** of the charge, s.100 protects him; otherwise the charge follows the land.
3. A registered decree or possession may give notice.
4. s.39 TPA also lets maintenance claims be enforced against a transferee with notice or a gratuitous transferee.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Calling every security a mortgage. If there is no transfer of interest, it is a charge.

quiz.why: Section 100 says no charge is enforceable against property in the hands of a transferee for consideration without notice, save as provided by law.

questions.why: Section 55(1)(a) requires disclosure of material defects the buyer could not discover with ordinary care.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Lease, exchange, gift and actionable claims (ss. 105–137)
courses.summary: Lease and licence distinctions, duration and notice, rights and liabilities of lessor and lessee, determination and holding over; exchange; gift, its formalities, onerous gifts and revocation; transfer of actionable claims.
outcomes: Define a lease and distinguish it from a licence
Calculate the notice period required under s.106
Apply the grounds of determination of lease in s.111
State the formalities of a valid gift under ss.122–123
Explain transfer of actionable claims under s.130

scenes.text: Pooja rents a shop at ₹30,000 a month on an oral understanding, paying rent monthly.
The landlord sends a notice to vacate in 15 days. Is that enough?

steps.title: Section 105
steps.body: A **lease** of immovable property is a transfer of a **right to enjoy** such property, made for a certain time, express or implied, or in perpetuity, in consideration of a price paid or promised, or of money, a share of crops, service or any other thing of value, to be rendered periodically or on specified occasions. Parties: lessor, lessee; consideration: premium (lump sum) and rent (periodic).

steps.title: Duration and notice (s.106, as amended 2002)
steps.body:
In the absence of contract or local law:
- Lease for **agricultural or manufacturing** purposes → year to year, terminable by **six months'** notice.
- Lease for **any other purpose** → month to month, terminable by **fifteen days'** notice.
Notice must be in writing, signed and sent by post or delivered/affixed. A notice is not invalid merely because the period mentioned falls short, if the suit is filed after the statutory period expires.

**s.107**: a lease from year to year, or for any term exceeding one year, or reserving a yearly rent, can be made **only by a registered instrument**.

steps.title: Solving Pooja's case
steps.body:
1. Oral lease, rent monthly, shop (commercial, not manufacturing) → month to month.
2. Required notice: 15 days in writing.
3. Landlord's 15-day written notice is valid under s.106 (subject to any State rent control law, which may give extra protection).
4. If the lease were for 3 years, it would need a registered deed; an unregistered one may still show the character of possession.

steps.title: Lease vs licence
steps.body: A **licence** (Easements Act s.52) grants permission to do something on land which would otherwise be unlawful, and creates **no interest** in the property. Test: substance of the agreement, intention, exclusive possession (important but not conclusive). See Associated Hotels of India v R.N. Kapoor (SC 1959).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying the old 'end of tenancy month' rule – removed in 2002.
- Assuming exclusive possession always means a lease.

activity.prompt: Tick the elements of a lease under s.105
items: Transfer of a right to enjoy immovable property
For a certain time or in perpetuity
Consideration: premium, rent or other value
Acceptance of the transfer by the lessee

quiz.why: Section 106 as amended in 2002 prescribes fifteen days' notice for leases other than agricultural or manufacturing.

quiz.why: Section 107 requires a registered instrument for leases exceeding one year.

quiz.q: A licence creates
quiz.why: Section 52 of the Easements Act defines licence as a personal permission that creates no estate or interest.

lessons.title: Rights, liabilities and determination of leases (ss. 108–117)

scenes.text: Raj's 11-month lease of a flat expires. He keeps paying rent and the landlord keeps accepting it.
Six months later the landlord files for eviction, calling him a trespasser.

steps.title: Section 108 – key rights and duties
steps.body:
Lessor: disclose material latent defects; put lessee in possession on request; covenant for quiet enjoyment.
Lessee: pay rent; keep property in good condition (fair wear and tear excepted); give notice of encroachment; not use for other purpose; not commit waste; may sub-let or assign absent a contract to the contrary; restore possession on determination. If property is destroyed by fire, tempest, flood etc. and becomes substantially unfit, the lease is voidable at the lessee's option.

steps.title: Section 111 – determination
steps.body: (a) efflux of time; (b) happening of a specified event; (c) interest of lessor terminating; (d) merger; (e) express surrender; (f) implied surrender; (g) forfeiture – breach of express condition with re-entry clause, lessee renouncing character by setting up title in a third person or himself, or lessee adjudicated insolvent where so provided – followed by written notice; (h) expiry of a notice to quit.

steps.title: Holding over – Raj
steps.body:
1. Lease expired by efflux of time (s.111(a)).
2. Raj stayed; landlord **accepted rent** = assent to continuance.
3. s.116: the lease is renewed from year to year or month to month according to purpose (s.106).
4. Residential → month to month; landlord must give 15 days' notice before suing; Raj is not a trespasser.
If the landlord had refused rent, Raj would be a **tenant at sufferance**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forfeiture is not automatic: lessor must give written notice of intention to determine.
- Relief against forfeiture for non-payment of rent is available under s.114 if arrears and costs are paid.

quiz.why: Section 116 renews the lease on a periodic basis when the lessor assents by accepting rent.

options: Lessee and lessor interests vest in one person
quiz.why: Section 111(d) ends the lease when the interests of lessee and lessor in the whole property become vested in the same person.

lessons.title: Gift: formalities, onerous gifts and revocation (ss. 122–129)

story.title: The flat gifted on a birthday

scenes.text: Mohan signs a registered gift deed of his flat in favour of his niece Riya, attested by two witnesses.
Mohan dies two days later, before Riya knew about the deed. Riya accepts it at the funeral.

steps.title: Section 122
steps.body: **Gift** is the transfer of certain existing movable or immovable property made **voluntarily and without consideration** by the donor to the donee, and **accepted** by or on behalf of the donee. Acceptance must be made **during the lifetime of the donor and while he is still capable of giving**. If the donee dies before acceptance, the gift is void.

steps.title: Section 123 – how made
steps.body:
- Immovable property: **registered instrument signed by or on behalf of the donor and attested by at least two witnesses**.
- Movable property: by registered instrument as above **or by delivery**.
**s.124**: gift of existing and future property – void as to future property.
**s.126**: gift may be suspended or revoked on a specified event agreed by both (not wholly at donor's will), or in cases where it could be rescinded if a contract (e.g., fraud, coercion).
**s.127**: onerous gift – donee who accepts must take the burden too.
**s.129**: does not affect donatio mortis causa or Muslim law.

steps.title: Solving Riya's case
steps.body:
1. Registered deed, signed, two attesting witnesses ✔.
2. Acceptance: must be during donor's lifetime. Riya accepted after Mohan died ✘.
3. Unless there is evidence of earlier acceptance (e.g., her receipt of the deed or conduct, or acceptance on her behalf), the gift fails.
Lesson: acceptance can be express or implied, and possession of the deed during the donor's life is strong evidence.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking delivery of possession is essential for immovables – registration and acceptance suffice under s.123.
- Thinking a donor can revoke whenever he likes – s.126 forbids revocation at the donor's mere will.

quiz.why: Section 124 makes a gift void to the extent it comprises future property.

quiz.q: Attesting witnesses needed for a gift of immovables
quiz.why: Section 123 requires attestation by at least two witnesses.

quiz.q: If the donee dies before acceptance, the gift
quiz.why: Section 122 states that if the donee dies before acceptance, the gift is void.

scenes.text: A supplier is owed ₹5 lakh by a retailer and sells this receivable to a factoring firm for ₹4.6 lakh.
The retailer, unaware, pays the supplier. Is the retailer discharged?

steps.title: Exchange (s.118)
steps.body: When two persons mutually transfer the **ownership of one thing for the ownership of another**, neither or both being money only, it is an exchange. It is made in the manner of a sale (registration rules apply). Each party has the rights and liabilities of a seller and buyer for what he gives and takes.

steps.title: Actionable claim (s.3, s.130)
steps.body:
An **actionable claim** is a claim to any **debt** (other than one secured by mortgage, hypothecation or pledge of movables) or to any **beneficial interest in movable property not in possession** of the claimant, which civil courts recognise as affording grounds for relief.

s.130: transfer must be by an **instrument in writing** signed by the transferor; it is complete on execution. Notice to the debtor is not needed for validity, but **a debtor who pays the transferor without notice is discharged** (s.130 read with illustrations).

steps.title: Solving the factoring case
steps.body:
1. ₹5 lakh unsecured trade debt = actionable claim.
2. Written assignment to the factor → complete between assignor and assignee.
3. Retailer had no notice and paid the supplier in good faith → retailer is discharged.
4. The factor must recover from the supplier. Lesson: assignees should give written notice to the debtor at once.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling a mortgage debt an actionable claim – secured debts are excluded.
- Confusing actionable claim with a mere right to sue for damages (non-transferable under s.6(e)).

questions.why: Without the lessor's assent the holding-over tenant has no renewed lease.

courses.title: Unit 5 · Easements and licences (Indian Easements Act, 1882)
courses.summary: Definition and essentials of easements, their classification, acquisition by grant, necessity, quasi-easement and prescription, extinction and suspension, and the law of licences including revocability.
outcomes: State the essentials of an easement under s.4
Classify easements as continuous/discontinuous and apparent/non-apparent
Apply s.13 (necessity, quasi-easement) and s.15 (prescription)
Identify modes of extinction of easements
Distinguish a licence from an easement and a lease, and apply s.60 on revocation

lessons.title: Nature, essentials and kinds of easements (ss. 4–7)

scenes.text: For decades the owners of a hill-top house have walked across a neighbour's orchard to reach the village road.
The new orchard owner builds a fence. The house owner claims a right of way.

steps.title: Section 4
steps.body:
An **easement** is a right which the owner or occupier of certain land possesses, as such, for the **beneficial enjoyment** of that land, to do and continue to do something, or to prevent and continue to prevent something being done, **in or upon, or in respect of, certain other land not his own**.
The land benefited = **dominant heritage**; the land burdened = **servient heritage**.

steps.title: Essentials
steps.body:
1. A dominant and a servient heritage.
2. Different owners (no one has an easement over his own land).
3. Right must be for beneficial enjoyment of the dominant heritage (accommodates it).
4. Right to do something or prevent something on the servient land.
5. The right must not amount to ownership or exclusive possession of the servient land.
6. Must be certain and capable of grant.

steps.title: Kinds (s.5)
steps.body:
- **Continuous**: enjoyment may be continual without act of man – e.g., right to light through a window, a drain.
- **Discontinuous**: needs act of man each time – e.g., right of way.
- **Apparent**: shown by a permanent sign visible on careful inspection – e.g., a worn path, a window.
- **Non-apparent**: no such sign – e.g., right to prevent building above a certain height.
Also positive/negative and affirmative easements; s.7 lists natural rights (e.g., lateral support, natural flow of water) which are not easements.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling a natural right (support of land in its natural state) an easement.
- Thinking a right of way is continuous – it is discontinuous because it needs a person to walk.

activity.prompt: Tick each essential of an easement
items: Dominant heritage and servient heritage exist
They are owned by different persons
The right benefits the dominant land
The right does not amount to ownership of the servient land
The right is certain and definite

quiz.q: A right of way is
quiz.why: It needs an act of man each time it is used, which makes it discontinuous under s.5.

quiz.q: The land that bears the burden is the
quiz.why: Section 4 calls the land on which liability is imposed the servient heritage.

quiz.q: Right of lateral support of land in its natural state is
quiz.why: Section 7 illustrations treat support of land in its natural condition as a natural incident of ownership, not an easement.

lessons.title: Acquisition: grant, necessity, quasi-easement and prescription (ss. 8–19)

scenes.text: A landowner sells the back half of his field. The back half has no access to any road except over the front half he keeps.
Separately, a shopkeeper has received light through a window for 22 years and the neighbour now plans a tower.

steps.title: Modes of acquisition
steps.body:
- **Express grant** by the owner of the servient land (s.8).
- **Easement of necessity** (s.13): on transfer or partition, if an easement is **absolutely necessary** for enjoying the dominant heritage, it is implied – e.g., access to landlocked land.
- **Quasi-easement** (s.13): an apparent and continuous easement necessary for enjoying the property as it was enjoyed at the time of transfer.
- **Prescription** (s.15).
- **Custom** (s.18).

steps.title: Prescription (s.15)
steps.body:
Light/air to a building, support, and other easements are acquired if enjoyed:
- **peaceably**, 
- **openly** (for other easements),
- **as an easement and as of right**,
- **without interruption**,
- for **20 years** (30 years where the servient owner is the Government).
The period must end within two years before the suit. Interruption means obstruction acquiesced in for one year after knowledge.

steps.title: Solving both cases
steps.body:
Landlocked plot: absolute necessity on transfer → easement of necessity over the front half (s.13). It ends when the necessity ends (s.41), e.g., a new public road opens.

Shopkeeper: 22 years of peaceable, uninterrupted enjoyment of light as of right → prescriptive easement of light (s.15). He can restrain building that would substantially diminish light so as to cause material interference with ordinary comfort or business (s.33), not any reduction at all.

scenes.text: A college permits a caterer to run a canteen in its hall; the caterer spends ₹12 lakh building a permanent kitchen with the college's knowledge.

steps.title: Section 52
steps.body: A **licence** is a grant by one person to another of a right to do, or continue to do, in or upon the immovable property of the grantor, something which would otherwise be unlawful, and which does **not amount to an easement or an interest in the property**. It is personal (s.56: not transferable) and does not bind transferees of the grantor generally.

steps.title: Revocation (s.60, s.64)
steps.body:
A licence may be revoked **except**:
(a) where it is **coupled with a transfer of property** and the transfer is in force; or
(b) where the licensee, **acting upon the licence, has executed a work of a permanent character and incurred expenses** in its execution.
**s.64**: a licensee for consideration evicted before fully enjoying the licence without his own fault may recover compensation from the grantor.

steps.title: Solving the canteen case
steps.body:
1. Permission to run a canteen = licence (no interest in the hall).
2. Caterer, acting on the licence, built a permanent kitchen at ₹12 lakh with the college's knowledge.
3. s.60(b) applies → licence irrevocable (courts examine whether the work was of a permanent character and done on the strength of the licence).
Otherwise the college could revoke, but s.64 compensation might be claimed if it was for consideration.

steps.body: Lease = interest, transferable, s.105 TPA | Licence = personal permission, s.52 | Easement = right attached to dominant land, s.4 | Charge = security without transfer, s.100 | Mortgage = transfer of interest for security, s.58.

lessons.title: Nature and basis of international law

scenes.text: A student asks: there is no world parliament, no world police and the ICJ cannot jail anyone. So is international law only 'positive morality'?
Yet every day thousands of flights cross borders under treaties that States follow.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body: Classical (Oppenheim): the body of customary and treaty rules considered legally binding by States in their intercourse with each other. Modern: rules governing relations of States, international organisations and, in certain respects, individuals and other non-State entities.

steps.title: Austin's objection and replies
steps.body:
Austin: law is a command of a sovereign backed by sanction; international law lacks both, so it is 'positive international morality'.
Replies: (1) Law need not depend on a sovereign command – customary law in societies existed without legislatures (Hart: a system of primary rules). (2) Sanctions exist: Chapter VII Security Council measures, countermeasures, self-defence, reputational and reciprocal pressure. (3) States treat it as law: they argue in legal terms and rarely claim a right to break it. (4) Courts apply it (ICJ, national courts).

steps.title: Theories of basis
steps.body:
- Naturalist: derived from natural law/reason (Grotius, 'father of international law', De Jure Belli ac Pacis, 1625).
- Positivist: based on consent of States (Lotus case, PCIJ 1927: restrictions on independence of States cannot be presumed).
- Modern: combination; jus cogens shows limits to pure consent.

steps.title: Short-note outline (5 marks)
steps.body: 'International law is the vanishing point of jurisprudence' (Holland) – explain the claim, give Austin's view, refute with Hart and State practice, conclude that it is a weak but real legal system (decentralised enforcement).

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Saying international law has no enforcement at all. Enforcement is decentralised, not absent.

steps.title: Article 38(1)
Custom: two elements
steps.body:
1. **State practice** (objective): extensive, virtually uniform, consistent (Asylum case, 1950: Colombia failed to prove a constant and uniform usage).
2. **Opinio juris** (subjective): belief the practice is legally required (North Sea Continental Shelf, 1969: equidistance in Article 6 of the 1958 Convention was not custom).
Persistent objector may avoid a new custom if it objects consistently from the start (Anglo-Norwegian Fisheries, 1951). Local/regional custom is possible (Right of Passage over Indian Territory, Portugal v India, 1960).

steps.title: Jus cogens
steps.body: Peremptory norms accepted by the international community as a whole from which no derogation is permitted (Article 53 VCLT). Examples: prohibition of aggression, genocide, slavery, torture, racial discrimination, the right of self-determination. A treaty conflicting with jus cogens is void.

steps.title: Worked application
steps.body: Fishing dispute, no treaty: (a) none; (b) look for customary rules on EEZ rights – UNCLOS provisions on EEZ widely reflect custom (Libya/Malta, 1985); (c) general principles such as good faith, estoppel; (d) earlier ICJ cases (Fisheries Jurisdiction) and writings to identify the rules.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Saying ICJ decisions are binding precedent. Article 59: a decision binds only the parties and that case.

lessons.title: Monism, dualism and international law in India

scenes.text: In 1997 there was no Indian law against sexual harassment at the workplace.
The Supreme Court used CEDAW, a treaty India had ratified, to frame binding guidelines. How?

steps.title: Theories
steps.body:
- **Monism** (Kelsen): one legal order; international law prevails and applies directly.
- **Dualism** (Triepel, Anzilotti): two separate orders; international law must be transformed into municipal law.
- **Transformation vs incorporation**: UK treats custom as part of common law (incorporation; Trendtex, 1977) but treaties need an Act (transformation).

steps.title: Indian position
steps.body:
- Article 51(c): State shall endeavour to foster respect for international law and treaty obligations (DPSP).
- Article 73 and 253: executive makes treaties; Parliament may legislate to implement any treaty.
- Treaties do not automatically become domestic law where they affect rights or need legislation (Maganbhai Ishwarbhai Patel v Union of India, 1969; Jolly George Varghese v Bank of Cochin, 1980 – municipal law prevails in conflict).
- But courts read treaties into fundamental rights where there is no conflicting law: **Vishaka v State of Rajasthan (1997)**, NALSA v Union of India (2014).
- Customary international law is part of Indian law unless contrary to domestic law (Vellore Citizens, 1996; People's Union for Civil Liberties v Union of India, 1997).

steps.title: Worked application
steps.body: A tribunal is asked to apply the Convention against Torture (India signed in 1997 but has not ratified). Since unratified, it is not binding as a treaty; but the prohibition of torture is customary and jus cogens, and courts read it into Article 21 (D.K. Basu, 1997, on custodial violence).

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Saying India is purely monist or purely dualist. India is broadly dualist for treaties but follows incorporation for custom and uses treaties to interpret rights.

scenes.text: A province declares independence, raises a flag and is recognised by 30 States but not by its parent State.
Is it a State? Does recognition create it, or merely acknowledge it?

steps.title: Montevideo Convention 1933, Article 1
steps.body: A State should possess: (a) a permanent population; (b) a defined territory (boundaries need not be fully settled); (c) government (effective control); (d) capacity to enter into relations with other States (independence). Modern additions debated: legality of creation (no use of force or violation of self-determination – e.g. non-recognition of Southern Rhodesia, Northern Cyprus).

steps.title: Theories of recognition
steps.body:
- **Constitutive** (Oppenheim, Lauterpacht – duty to recognise): recognition creates statehood.
- **Declaratory** (prevailing; Montevideo Art. 3 – 'political existence of the State is independent of recognition'): recognition acknowledges an existing fact.
**De jure** (full, permanent) vs **de facto** (provisional; government not yet firmly established). Express or implied (e.g. concluding a bilateral treaty, establishing diplomatic relations). Recognition of governments: Estrada doctrine (Mexico, 1930) – avoid formal recognition, just maintain or withdraw relations; Tobar doctrine – recognise only constitutionally established governments.

steps.title: Applying to the province
steps.body: Population and territory: yes. Government: is it effective without foreign military support? Independence: if it depends on another State's army, it may be a puppet. Recognition by 30 States is evidence but, on the declaratory view, not decisive. ICJ Kosovo Advisory Opinion (2010): the declaration of independence did not violate general international law, but the Court did not decide on statehood.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Saying UN membership is a requirement for statehood. Switzerland joined only in 2002 but was a State long before.

steps.title: Bases of prescriptive jurisdiction
steps.body:
1. **Territorial** – subjective (act begins in the territory) and objective (effects/completion in the territory; Lotus case).
2. **Nationality** (active personality) – over nationals abroad.
3. **Passive personality** – over offences against nationals abroad (accepted for terrorism, etc.).
4. **Protective** – acts abroad threatening the State's security or vital interests (counterfeiting currency).
5. **Universality** – piracy, war crimes, genocide, crimes against humanity, torture – any State may try (Eichmann, Israel, 1961).
Enforcement jurisdiction is strictly territorial: a State cannot arrest in another State's territory without consent.

steps.title: Indian law examples
steps.body: Section 75 of the Information Technology Act 2000 applies to offences outside India involving a computer system in India. The BNS 2023 (like IPC ss. 3–4) extends to offences by Indian citizens outside India and on Indian ships/aircraft.

steps.title: Worked application
steps.body: Hacker case: objective territorial principle (effects in India) and IT Act s. 75 give prescriptive jurisdiction; passive personality also supports. Enforcement: India cannot arrest him in X; it must seek extradition or mutual legal assistance.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Mixing up prescriptive and enforcement jurisdiction. Having the right to legislate does not give a right to arrest abroad.

steps.title: Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations 1961
steps.body:
- Premises of the mission are **inviolable** (Art. 22).
- Diplomatic bag not to be opened or detained (Art. 27).
- Person of a diplomatic agent is inviolable; no arrest or detention (Art. 29).
- Immunity from criminal jurisdiction (absolute) and civil/administrative jurisdiction subject to exceptions: private immovable property, succession, private professional/commercial activity (Art. 31).
- Only the sending State can **waive** immunity, expressly (Art. 32).
- Receiving State may declare a diplomat **persona non grata** at any time without reasons (Art. 9).
India implements it by the Diplomatic Relations (Vienna Convention) Act 1972.

steps.title: State immunity
steps.body: Absolute theory (older) vs **restrictive theory**: immunity for sovereign acts (acta jure imperii) but not commercial acts (acta jure gestionis). India: section 86 CPC – a foreign State may be sued only with consent of the Central Government. ICJ Jurisdictional Immunities (Germany v Italy, 2012): immunity applies even to claims of serious violations by armed forces. Arrest Warrant case (DRC v Belgium, 2002): sitting foreign minister immune from foreign criminal jurisdiction.

steps.title: Applying it
steps.body: India cannot arrest or prosecute the diplomat (Arts. 29, 31). Options: request waiver from the sending State; declare him persona non grata; the sending State may prosecute him at home (Art. 31(4)); victim may claim insurance/compensation via the mission.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Thinking the diplomat can waive his own immunity. Immunity belongs to the sending State.

steps.title: State succession
steps.body: Vienna Convention on Succession of States in respect of Treaties 1978: newly independent States start with a 'clean slate' (Art. 16), but boundary treaties continue (Art. 11). India continued British India's international personality and UN membership; Pakistan was admitted as a new member. Succession to debts, property and archives: Vienna Convention 1983 (not widely ratified).

steps.title: Subjects beyond States
steps.body:
- **International organisations**: Reparation for Injuries case (1949) – the UN has international legal personality and can claim for injuries to its agents.
- **Individuals**: duties (Nuremberg, ICTY, ICTR, ICC) and rights (human rights treaties with individual complaint procedures).
- Others: Holy See, ICRC, insurgents and national liberation movements (limited personality).

steps.body: A newly independent island State asks whether it is bound by a fisheries treaty and a boundary treaty signed by the former colonial power. Fisheries: clean slate, it may choose to notify succession. Boundary: continues (Art. 11), reinforcing uti possidetis (Burkina Faso/Mali, 1986).

scenes.text: A Foreign Minister signs a treaty in Geneva. Back home, Parliament has not approved it.
Is her State bound now? And can it sign with a reservation excluding one article?

steps.title: Key VCLT rules
steps.body:
- Treaty: an international agreement concluded between States in written form and governed by international law (Art. 2(1)(a)).
- Full powers (Art. 7): Heads of State, Heads of Government and Foreign Ministers need none.
- Consent to be bound by signature, exchange, **ratification**, acceptance, approval or **accession** (Arts. 11–15).
- Obligation not to defeat the object and purpose before entry into force once signed (Art. 18).
- **Pacta sunt servanda** (Art. 26): every treaty in force is binding and must be performed in good faith. A party may not invoke internal law to justify failure (Art. 27).

steps.title: Reservations (Arts. 19–23)
steps.body: A unilateral statement excluding or modifying the legal effect of certain provisions. Not allowed if prohibited by the treaty, or incompatible with its **object and purpose** (Reservations to the Genocide Convention Advisory Opinion, 1951). An objecting State may still be in treaty relations with the reserving State unless it opposes entry into force; the reserved provision then does not apply between them to the extent of the reservation (Art. 21(3)). Distinguish an **interpretative declaration**, which only clarifies meaning. Indian example: on ratifying CEDAW (1993) India made declarations on Articles 5(a) and 16(1) and a reservation to Article 29(1) (ICJ dispute settlement).

steps.title: Applying it
steps.body: Minister signs a treaty subject to ratification: the State is not yet bound by the treaty but must not defeat its object and purpose (Art. 18) until it makes clear it will not ratify. A reservation excluding the core obligation of a human-rights treaty would be incompatible with object and purpose.

scenes.text: A foreign research vessel is 30 nautical miles off India's baseline, surveying the seabed for oil.

steps.title: Zones measured from baselines
steps.body:
- **Internal waters**: landward of baselines – full sovereignty.
- **Territorial sea**: up to **12 nm** – sovereignty, subject to **innocent passage** (Arts. 17–19).
- **Contiguous zone**: up to **24 nm** – control to prevent/punish infringement of customs, fiscal, immigration, sanitary laws (Art. 33).
- **EEZ**: up to **200 nm** – sovereign rights for exploring, exploiting, conserving natural resources; jurisdiction over artificial islands, marine scientific research, environment (Arts. 55–57). Other States: freedom of navigation and overflight.
- **Continental shelf**: natural prolongation to the outer edge of the margin or 200 nm, up to 350 nm or 100 nm from the 2,500 m isobath (Art. 76).
- **High seas**: freedoms; flag-State jurisdiction; universal jurisdiction over piracy.
- **The Area** (deep seabed beyond national jurisdiction): common heritage of mankind (Art. 136), managed by the ISA.
India: Territorial Waters, Continental Shelf, Exclusive Economic Zone and Other Maritime Zones Act 1976.

steps.title: Worked numerical
steps.body:
Vessel at 30 nm: beyond 12 nm (not territorial sea) and beyond 24 nm (not contiguous zone), but within 200 nm → EEZ. Marine scientific research in the EEZ requires coastal State consent (Art. 246). India can require it to stop and leave or seek consent.
Conversion: 1 nm = 1.852 km, so 200 nm = 370.4 km; 12 nm = 22.224 km.

steps.title: Innocent passage
steps.body: Passage is innocent so long as not prejudicial to peace, good order or security; Article 19(2) lists non-innocent activities (weapons exercise, spying, propaganda, loading persons contrary to laws, wilful serious pollution, fishing, research or survey activities). Submarines must navigate on the surface and show their flag (Art. 20). Corfu Channel (1949): warships have a right of innocent passage through international straits.

scenes.text: In 1979, students stormed the US embassy in Tehran and held diplomats hostage. Iran's government later endorsed their action.

steps.title: ARSIWA 2001
steps.body:
Every internationally wrongful act of a State entails its responsibility (Art. 1). Elements (Art. 2): conduct (act or omission) **attributable** to the State and constituting a **breach** of an international obligation.
Attribution: State organs, including ultra vires acts (Arts. 4, 7); persons exercising governmental authority (5); persons acting on instructions or under the **direction or control** of the State (8 – Nicaragua 'effective control' test; ICTY Tadić used 'overall control'); conduct acknowledged and adopted by the State (11 – Tehran Hostages, 1980).

steps.title: Circumstances precluding wrongfulness
steps.body: Consent (20), self-defence (21), countermeasures (22), force majeure (23), distress (24), necessity (25 – only to safeguard an essential interest against grave and imminent peril, Gabčíkovo). None justifies breach of jus cogens (26).

steps.title: Reparation
steps.body: Full reparation (Chorzów Factory, PCIJ 1928): restitution, compensation, satisfaction (Arts. 34–37). Cessation and guarantees of non-repetition (30). Diplomatic protection of nationals needs **nationality** with genuine link (Nottebohm, 1955) and **exhaustion of local remedies**; Barcelona Traction (1970) – company's State of incorporation, not shareholders' State; also introduced obligations **erga omnes**.

steps.title: Applying to Tehran
steps.body: Phase 1: Iran failed to protect the embassy (omission by its organs – breach of VCDR Arts. 22, 29). Phase 2: Iran's endorsement turned the students' continued occupation into acts of the State (adoption). Result: responsibility and duty of reparation.

steps.title: Article 2(4) UN Charter
steps.body: All members shall refrain from the threat or use of force against the territorial integrity or political independence of any State, or in any other manner inconsistent with the UN's purposes. It is customary and widely considered jus cogens.

steps.title: Exceptions
steps.body:
1. **Self-defence (Art. 51)**: inherent right if an **armed attack** occurs, until the Security Council acts; must be reported to the UNSC. Customary requirements: **necessity** and **proportionality** (Caroline incident, 1837 – necessity 'instant, overwhelming, leaving no choice of means'; Nicaragua; Oil Platforms, 2003). Armed attack means the 'most grave forms' of force (Nicaragua). Anticipatory self-defence against imminent attack is debated; pre-emptive force against remote threats is not accepted.
2. **Security Council authorisation under Chapter VII**: Art. 39 determination of a threat to peace, breach or act of aggression; Art. 41 non-forcible measures (sanctions); Art. 42 military measures (e.g. Resolution 678 (1990) on Iraq–Kuwait).
Debated: humanitarian intervention; Responsibility to Protect (2005 World Summit – collective action through the UNSC).

steps.title: Applying it
steps.body: State A: (1) Is there an armed attack? Yes, if scale and effects are grave. (2) Attribution: if B does not control the groups, the 'unwilling or unable' doctrine is invoked by some States but remains contested; Armed Activities (DRC v Uganda, 2005) found no right to self-defence against DRC for attacks by irregulars not attributable to DRC. (3) Necessity and proportionality of strikes. (4) Report to UNSC under Art. 51.

steps.title: ICJ jurisdiction
steps.body: Contentious – only States; consent required through: special agreement (compromis); **compromissory clause** in a treaty (Art. 36(1)); **optional clause** declarations (Art. 36(2)), often with reservations; forum prorogatum. Advisory opinions (Art. 65; Charter Art. 96) on request of the GA, SC or authorised agencies. Provisional measures (Art. 41) are binding (LaGrand, 2001). Merits: Pakistan breached Article 36 VCCR by not informing Jadhav of his rights, not notifying India without delay and denying consular access. scenes.text: A businessman accused of a large bank fraud flees from India to the UK.

steps.title: Principles
steps.body:
Extradition is the surrender of an accused or convicted person by one State to another. Generally treaty-based. Principles:
- **Double criminality**: act must be an offence in both States.
- **Speciality**: person may be tried only for the offence for which extradited.
- **Political offence exception** (excluded for terrorism under many treaties).
- Prima facie case or sufficient evidence (depending on treaty).
- Non-extradition of nationals in some States; aut dedere aut judicare (extradite or prosecute) for certain crimes.

steps.title: Extradition Act 1962
steps.body: Applies to treaty States and, by notification, to others under arrangements. Section 31 restricts surrender for political offences, time-barred offences and where speciality would not be respected. Section 34C: a person extradited to India for an offence punishable with death, by a State whose law does not provide the death penalty, is liable only to imprisonment for life. The Fugitive Economic Offenders Act 2018 allows declaring a person a fugitive economic offender (scheduled offences of ₹100 crore or more) and confiscating property.

steps.title: Applying it
steps.body: UK court (Westminster Magistrates) checks: extradition offence under the India–UK treaty (1992); double criminality (fraud is an offence in both); prima facie case; bars such as human rights (Article 3 ECHR – prison conditions); then Home Secretary's order; appeal to High Court. Such cases often take many years.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Saying extradition is a customary duty. There is no general customary obligation to extradite; it rests on treaties or arrangements.

steps.title: Asylum
steps.body: **Territorial asylum**: granted within the State's territory – a right of the State, not of the individual (UNGA Declaration on Territorial Asylum 1967; UDHR Art. 14 – right to seek and enjoy asylum). **Diplomatic (extra-territorial) asylum** in embassies is not generally recognised except in Latin American regional practice (Asylum case, 1950).

steps.title: Refugees
steps.body: 1951 Convention and 1967 Protocol: refugee = person outside country of nationality with a well-founded fear of persecution for reasons of race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular social group or political opinion. **Non-refoulement** (Art. 33): no return to territories where life or freedom would be threatened – widely regarded as customary. India is not a party, but Indian courts have applied Article 21 to protect foreigners' lives (NHRC v State of Arunachal Pradesh, 1996, Chakma refugees).

steps.title: Nationality
steps.body: Acquired by birth (jus soli / jus sanguinis), descent, naturalisation, registration. Statelessness: 1954 and 1961 Conventions. India: Citizenship Act 1955 – citizenship by birth now also depends on parents' citizenship status (amendments of 1986 and 2003).

scenes.text: A municipal body levies a 'development fee' on shops by a mere resolution, with no Act authorising it.
Shopkeepers challenge it. What does the Constitution say?

steps.title: Core provisions
steps.body:
- **Article 265**: no tax shall be levied or collected except by authority of law (a valid law made by a competent legislature).
- Union List taxes include taxes on income other than agricultural income (Entry 82), customs (83), corporation tax (85), taxes on capital value of assets (86).
- State List: agricultural income (46), land and buildings (49), alcohol excise (51), taxes on entertainment by local bodies, etc.
- **Article 246A** (101st Amendment, 2016): Parliament and State legislatures both have power to make laws on GST; Parliament exclusively for inter-State supply (IGST, Art. 269A). GST Council under **Article 279A**.
- Article 289: Union cannot tax State property and income (subject to trade/business exceptions); Article 285: States cannot tax Union property.

steps.title: Tax vs fee
steps.body: A tax is a compulsory exaction for public purposes without direct quid pro quo; a fee is charged for a special service rendered (Commissioner, Hindu Religious Endowments v Sri Lakshmindra Thirtha Swamiar (Shirur Mutt), 1954). A fee needs a broad correlation with the service, not exact equivalence.

steps.title: Definitions

- **Assessee** (s. 2(7)): person by whom tax is payable, including deemed and defaulting assessees.
- **Previous year** (s. 3): financial year (1 April–31 March) in which income is earned.
- **Assessment year** (s. 2(9)): the year following the previous year, in which income is assessed.
- **Income** (s. 2(24)): inclusive definition – profits, dividends, perquisites, capital gains, winnings from lotteries etc.
- **Charge** (s. 4): tax at rates in the Finance Act on total income of the previous year.

steps.title: Income-tax Act 2025

lessons.title: Lab: Residential status and scope of income

scenes.text: Mr Lee, a foreign national consultant, spent 100 days in India in FY 2025-26.
In the four preceding years he spent 120, 100, 90 and 80 days. Is he resident?

steps.title: Section 6(1) for individuals
steps.body:
Resident if in India for: (a) **182 days or more** in the previous year; or (b) **60 days or more** in the previous year **and 365 days or more** in the 4 preceding years.
Modifications to (b): for an Indian citizen leaving India for employment or as a crew member, and for an Indian citizen/PIO visiting India, 60 is replaced by 182; but for a visiting citizen/PIO with total income (other than foreign source) exceeding ₹15 lakh, 60 is replaced by **120**.
**Deemed resident** (s. 6(1A)): Indian citizen with such income above ₹15 lakh not liable to tax in any other country.
**Not ordinarily resident** (s. 6(6)): non-resident in 9 of 10 preceding years, or in India 729 days or less in the 7 preceding years, or the special 120-day/deemed-resident cases.

steps.title: Scope (section 5)
steps.body:
- ROR: global income.
- RNOR: income received/accruing in India plus foreign income from a business controlled or profession set up in India.
- Non-resident: only income received or deemed received in India, or accruing or deemed to accrue in India (s. 9).

steps.title: Worked computation
steps.body:
Mr Lee: 100 days < 182, so test (a) fails. Test (b): 100 ≥ 60 ✓; preceding 4 years = 120 + 100 + 90 + 80 = 390 ≥ 365 ✓ → **Resident**.
RNOR check: was he non-resident in 9 of 10 preceding years? He was non-resident in each of those years (all under 182 days, and earlier years insufficient) – if so, he is **RNOR**, taxable only on Indian income plus foreign income from an Indian-controlled business.

steps.title: Second example
steps.body: Anita, Indian citizen working in Dubai, visits India for 130 days in FY 2025-26; Indian-source income ₹18 lakh (rent and interest). Since she is a visiting citizen with Indian income > ₹15 lakh, the 60 is replaced by 120: 130 ≥ 120, and if she was in India 365+ days in the preceding 4 years she is resident – but such a person is treated as **RNOR** (s. 6(6)(c)).

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Counting the day of arrival and departure: both days are generally counted as days in India.

scenes.text: Foreign investors routed investments through Mauritius companies to use the India–Mauritius tax treaty exemption on capital gains.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body:
- **Tax planning**: arranging affairs within the law and its intent (claiming 80C deductions).
- **Tax avoidance**: legal but exploits loopholes against legislative intent.
- **Tax evasion**: illegal – concealment, false accounts; punishable (ss. 276C etc.).

steps.title: Leading cases
steps.body:
- **IRC v Duke of Westminster (1936)**: every man is entitled to order his affairs so that tax is less.
- **McDowell & Co v CTO (1985)**: colourable devices cannot be part of tax planning.
- **Union of India v Azadi Bachao Andolan (2003)**: upheld CBDT circular accepting Mauritius tax residency certificates; treaty shopping not per se illegal.
- **Vodafone International Holdings v Union of India (2012)**: offshore transfer of shares not taxable in India under then law; look at the transaction as a whole. Parliament responded with retrospective amendment to s. 9 (2012), later withdrawn by the Taxation Laws (Amendment) Act 2021.
- **GAAR** (Chapter X-A, ss. 95–102, from AY 2018-19): impermissible avoidance arrangements whose main purpose is a tax benefit and which lack commercial substance can be disregarded.

steps.title: Classify
steps.body: Investing ₹1.5 lakh in PPF for 80C under the old regime – planning. Creating a shell company in a treaty country with no staff solely to avoid capital gains tax – avoidance (GAAR/PPT risk). Showing fake purchase bills – evasion.

steps.title: Five heads (section 14)

4. Capital gains (ss. 45–55A)

scenes.text: Mr Rao lets out a flat for ₹30,000 per month, pays municipal tax of ₹20,000 and home-loan interest of ₹1,50,000 in FY 2025-26.

steps.title: Charge (section 22)
steps.body: Annual value of property consisting of buildings or land appurtenant, of which the assessee is owner, other than portions used for own business or profession, is taxable under this head.

steps.title: Computation
steps.body:
Gross Annual Value (GAV) = higher of expected rent (higher of municipal value and fair rent, capped at standard rent) and actual rent received/receivable (s. 23(1)).
Less municipal taxes **paid** by owner during the year → **Net Annual Value (NAV)**.
Less section 24: (a) **30% of NAV** standard deduction; (b) **interest on borrowed capital** (pre-construction interest allowed in 5 equal instalments from the year of completion).
Self-occupied (up to two houses): annual value nil (s. 23(2)); interest deduction capped at **₹2,00,000** (old regime); under the new regime no interest deduction for self-occupied property.

steps.title: Worked let-out
steps.body:
Actual rent = 30,000 × 12 = ₹3,60,000 (assume higher than expected rent) → GAV ₹3,60,000.
Less municipal tax ₹20,000 → NAV ₹3,40,000.
Less 30% × 3,40,000 = ₹1,02,000.
Less interest ₹1,50,000.
**Income from house property = ₹88,000.**

steps.title: Retirement benefits
steps.body:
- **Gratuity** (s. 10(10)): government employees fully exempt; employees covered by the Payment of Gratuity Act – least of actual, ₹20 lakh, and 15/26 × last drawn salary × years of service.
- **Leave encashment on retirement** (s. 10(10AA)): government employees fully exempt; others up to ₹25 lakh (from 1 April 2023) subject to formula.
- **Commuted pension** (s. 10(10A)): partially exempt for non-government employees.
- VRS compensation up to ₹5 lakh (s. 10(10C)).
These exemptions remain available under the new regime as well.

Covered employee: last drawn basic + DA ₹52,000/month; 30 years of service; gratuity received ₹10,00,000.
Formula: 15/26 × 52,000 × 30 = ₹9,00,000.
Exempt = least of 10,00,000; 20,00,000; 9,00,000 = **₹9,00,000**. Taxable = ₹1,00,000.

lessons.title: Business or profession: deductions and depreciation

scenes.text: A small engineering workshop buys a new lathe in November and pays a supplier ₹15,000 in cash.
How much depreciation can it claim, and is the cash payment allowed?

steps.title: Charge and deductions
steps.body: Section 28 charges profits of any business or profession. Deductions: rent, repairs, insurance (s. 30–31), **depreciation** (s. 32), scientific research (s. 35), and the residuary **section 37(1)** – any expenditure (not capital, not personal) laid out wholly and exclusively for the business. Expenditure for an offence or prohibited by law is not allowed (Explanation 1 to s. 37).

steps.title: Depreciation (section 32)
steps.body: Block of assets, written down value (WDV) method. Common rates: buildings (residential 5%, others 10%), furniture 10%, plant and machinery 15%, computers 40%. If an asset is acquired and put to use for **less than 180 days** in the year, only **half** the rate is allowed. Additional depreciation of 20% for new plant and machinery in manufacturing (s. 32(1)(iia)) – not available under certain concessional regimes.

steps.title: Worked depreciation
steps.body:
Plant block (15%): opening WDV ₹10,00,000; new lathe ₹4,00,000 bought and put to use on 1 November 2025 (used < 180 days).
- On opening WDV: 10,00,000 × 15% = ₹1,50,000
- On lathe: 4,00,000 × 7.5% = ₹30,000
Total depreciation = **₹1,80,000**; closing WDV = 14,00,000 − 1,80,000 = ₹12,20,000.

steps.title: Key disallowances
steps.body:
- **40(a)(ia)**: 30% of expenditure disallowed if TDS not deducted/paid.
- **40A(3)**: payments to a person in a day exceeding **₹10,000** otherwise than by account-payee cheque/draft/electronic modes are disallowed (₹35,000 for transporters).
- **43B**: certain sums (taxes, employer PF contributions, bonus, interest to banks, leave encashment, and payments to micro/small enterprises beyond MSMED Act time limits – s. 43B(h)) allowed only on actual payment.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Applying the half-rate rule to the opening WDV. It applies only to assets acquired and used less than 180 days in that year.

steps.title: Basics
steps.body:
Section 45: profits from transfer of a capital asset (s. 2(14)) are capital gains. Transfer (s. 2(47)) includes sale, exchange, relinquishment, compulsory acquisition.
**Holding period (from 23 July 2024)**: listed securities and units of equity-oriented funds – long-term if held **more than 12 months**; all other assets – **more than 24 months**.
Computation (s. 48): full value of consideration − expenses on transfer − cost of acquisition − cost of improvement.

steps.title: Rates for transfers on or after 23 July 2024
steps.body:
- **STCG on listed equity (s. 111A)**: 20%.
- **LTCG on listed equity (s. 112A)**: 12.5% on gains exceeding **₹1,25,000** in a year, no indexation; grandfathering of cost to 31 January 2018 value for older holdings.
- **Other LTCG (s. 112)**: 12.5% without indexation. For land or building acquired before 23 July 2024 by a resident individual/HUF, option to compute at 20% with indexation and pay the lower tax.
- Other STCG: normal slab rates.
Add 4% health and education cess (plus surcharge if applicable).

LTCG = ₹3,00,000. Exempt ₹1,25,000 → taxable ₹1,75,000.
Tax = 12.5% × 1,75,000 = ₹21,875; cess 4% = ₹875; **total ₹22,750**.

steps.body:

Without indexation: 70,00,000 − 1,00,000 − 40,00,000 = ₹29,00,000; tax at 12.5% = ₹3,62,500 (+ cess).
She may compare with 20% on indexed gain using Cost Inflation Index (CII 2019-20 = 289; 2025-26 = 376): indexed cost = 40,00,000 × 376 / 289 = ₹52,04,152 (rounded); indexed LTCG = 70,00,000 − 1,00,000 − 52,04,152 = ₹16,95,848; tax at 20% = ₹3,39,170. scenes.text: Arjun receives ₹80,000 from a college friend on his birthday and ₹2,00,000 from his uncle.
Are these taxable?

steps.title: Capital gains exemptions
steps.body:
- **Section 54**: LTCG on residential house reinvested in one residential house in India (purchase 1 year before or 2 years after, or construction within 3 years); option of two houses once if LTCG ≤ ₹2 crore; exemption capped so that cost of new house above **₹10 crore** is ignored.

steps.title: Main deductions (old regime)
steps.body:
- **80C**: up to ₹1,50,000 – PPF, EPF (employee share), ELSS, life insurance premium, tuition fees for 2 children, principal repayment of housing loan, 5-year bank FD, NSC, Sukanya Samriddhi.
- **80CCD(1B)**: additional ₹50,000 for NPS.
- **80D**: health insurance – ₹25,000 (self/family), additional ₹25,000 for parents (₹50,000 if parents are senior citizens).

- **80G**: donations (50% or 100%, with or without limit).

steps.title: Clubbing (ss. 60–64)
steps.body: Income of others included in the assessee's income: transfer of income without transfer of asset (s. 60); revocable transfers (s. 61–62); income from assets transferred to spouse without adequate consideration (s. 64(1)(iv)); minor child's income clubbed with the parent with higher income (s. 64(1A)), with ₹1,500 exemption per child (s. 10(32)), except income from the minor's own skill or manual work.

steps.title: Worked
steps.body: Husband gifts ₹10 lakh to wife; she invests in an FD earning ₹70,000 interest → clubbed with the husband's income (s. 64(1)(iv)). Minor daughter earns ₹20,000 interest on a deposit made by parents → ₹18,500 clubbed with the higher-income parent; if she earned ₹20,000 from her own singing performances, not clubbed.

steps.title: Assessments
steps.body:
- **143(1)**: summary processing (arithmetical errors, incorrect claims apparent).
- **143(3)**: scrutiny assessment – now largely **faceless (s. 144B)**.
- **144**: best-judgment assessment on non-compliance.
- **147/148/148A**: reassessment of income escaping assessment. After the Finance (No. 2) Act 2024 (notices from 1 September 2024): within **3 years** from end of the AY, or up to **5 years** if escaped income is ₹50 lakh or more; s. 148A procedure (show-cause and order) before notice.

steps.title: Appeals
steps.body:
1. **CIT(Appeals)** / JCIT(A) – s. 246A, within **30 days**.
2. **ITAT** – s. 253, within **60 days** (final fact-finding authority).
3. **High Court** – s. 260A, within **120 days**, only on a **substantial question of law**.
4. **Supreme Court** – s. 261 (certificate) or Article 136.
Alternatives: rectification (s. 154), revision (s. 263 against orders prejudicial to revenue; s. 264 on assessee's application), Vivad se Vishwas schemes.

steps.title: Laws
steps.body: Central GST Act 2017, State GST Acts, Integrated GST Act 2017, UTGST Act 2017, GST (Compensation to States) Act 2017. GST subsumed excise, service tax, VAT, entry tax etc. Outside GST: alcoholic liquor for human consumption; petroleum crude, high-speed diesel, petrol, natural gas and aviation turbine fuel (until the Council notifies); electricity.

steps.title: Supply (s. 7 CGST)
steps.body: All forms of supply of goods or services – sale, transfer, barter, exchange, licence, rental, lease – for consideration in the course or furtherance of business; import of services for consideration; activities in Schedule I even without consideration (e.g. supply between related persons, between distinct persons/branches); Schedule III – neither goods nor services (e.g. employee services to employer, actionable claims other than specified ones, sale of land and completed building).

steps.title: Intra-State vs inter-State
steps.body: Location of supplier and place of supply in the same State → **CGST + SGST** (equal halves). Different States, imports, exports, SEZ supplies → **IGST** (Art. 269A). Rates (after the GST Council's 56th meeting, effective 22 September 2025): main slabs **5% and 18%**, a **40%** rate for specified sin/luxury goods, plus special rates (e.g. 0.25%, 3% for gold), and exempt/nil items.

steps.body:
Pune trader sells goods worth ₹1,00,000 at 18%:
- To Pune buyer (intra-State): CGST 9% = ₹9,000 + SGST 9% = ₹9,000; invoice ₹1,18,000.
- To Bengaluru buyer (inter-State): IGST 18% = ₹18,000; invoice ₹1,18,000.

steps.title: Registration (s. 22, 24)
steps.body: Aggregate turnover threshold: **₹40 lakh** for exclusive suppliers of goods (in most States), **₹20 lakh** for services (₹10 lakh/₹20 lakh in special category States as notified). Compulsory registration regardless of turnover (s. 24): inter-State taxable supplies of goods, e-commerce sellers (with exceptions), casual taxable persons, reverse-charge recipients, input service distributors.

steps.title: Input tax credit (s. 16)
steps.body: Conditions: possession of tax invoice; receipt of goods/services; supplier has filed returns and tax reflected in GSTR-2B; tax actually paid to Government; return filed by recipient. Blocked credits (s. 17(5)): motor vehicles (with exceptions), food and beverages, club memberships, works contract for immovable property (except plant and machinery), goods for personal use, goods lost/stolen/gifted. Utilisation order: IGST credit first for IGST, then CGST and SGST; CGST credit cannot pay SGST and vice versa.

steps.title: Worked net liability
steps.body:
Turnover ₹60 lakh > ₹40 lakh → registration required.
Output tax on ₹5,00,000 at 18%: CGST ₹45,000 + SGST ₹45,000 = ₹90,000.
Input tax on wood ₹3,00,000 at 18%: CGST ₹27,000 + SGST ₹27,000 = ₹54,000.
Net payable in cash: CGST 45,000 − 27,000 = ₹18,000; SGST 45,000 − 27,000 = ₹18,000; **total ₹36,000**.

steps.title: Composition scheme (s. 10)
steps.body: For small taxpayers with turnover up to **₹1.5 crore** (₹75 lakh in special category States): manufacturers 1%, traders 1%, restaurants 5% (combined CGST+SGST); no ITC; cannot collect tax from customers; no inter-State outward supplies. Service providers' option up to ₹50 lakh at 6% (s. 10(2A)).

lessons.title: What is a tort? Elements and maxims

scenes.text: In Ashby v White (1703) a returning officer wrongly refused to let a qualified voter vote; his candidate still won.
The voter suffered no money loss, but his legal right was violated – he got damages. Injuria sine damno.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
Salmond: a civil wrong for which the remedy is an action for unliquidated damages, and which is not exclusively the breach of a contract or breach of trust or other merely equitable obligation.
Winfield: tortious liability arises from breach of a duty primarily fixed by law; this duty is towards persons generally and its breach is redressable by an action for unliquidated damages.
Elements: (1) wrongful act or omission by the defendant; (2) legal damage – violation of a legal right of the plaintiff; (3) legal remedy, typically unliquidated damages.

steps.title: Two maxims
steps.body:
**Injuria sine damno** – violation of a legal right without actual loss is actionable: Ashby v White; Bhim Singh v State of J&K (1985), MLA illegally detained to prevent him attending Assembly, ₹50,000 exemplary compensation.
**Damnum sine injuria** – actual loss without violation of a legal right is not actionable: Gloucester Grammar School case (1410), a rival school reduced fees; Mogul Steamship v McGregor Gow (1892), trade competition; Ushaben v Bhagyalaxmi Chitra Mandir (1978), film said to hurt religious feelings – no legal right infringed.

steps.title: Tort vs crime vs contract
steps.body:
Tort: duty fixed by law, owed to persons generally; remedy unliquidated damages; suit by injured person; can be compromised.
Crime: wrong against society; prosecuted by State; punishment.
Contract: duty fixed by parties, owed to specific persons; liquidated or unliquidated damages; privity needed.
The same act may be both (e.g. assault is a tort and an offence under BNS 2023).

steps.title: Law of tort or law of torts?
steps.body: Winfield's 'pigeon-hole' (general principle: all unjustified harm is tortious) vs Salmond's 'pigeon-hole' theory (only specific recognised torts). Modern law shows both: new torts are recognised (e.g. negligence in Donoghue), but not every harm is actionable.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Thinking motive matters: in general a lawful act does not become tortious because of a bad motive (Bradford Corporation v Pickles, 1895), except in torts like malicious prosecution.

story.title: The spectator hit by a car

scenes.text: At a car race, a car crashed into spectators.
In Hall v Brooklands Auto Racing Club (1933) spectators were held to have accepted such risks – volenti.

steps.title: Volenti
steps.body:
To a willing person, no injury is done. Consent may be express or implied, must be free, and relate to the risk of the act that occurred.
Cases: Hall v Brooklands (spectator); Padmavati v Dugganaika (1975), passengers who jumped from a jeep after it went out of control; Wooldridge v Sumner (1963).

steps.title: Limits
steps.body:
- Knowledge is not consent: scienti non fit injuria is NOT a rule (Smith v Baker, 1891 – workman aware of crane risk did not consent)
- Rescue cases: a rescuer is not volenti (Haynes v Harwood, 1935)
- Consent obtained by fraud is invalid (R v Williams, 1923)
- Unfair contract terms and statutory duties may limit it
- Negligence beyond the accepted risk is not covered (Slater v Clay Cross, 1956)

steps.title: Plaintiff the wrongdoer and contributory negligence
steps.body:
Ex turpi causa non oritur actio: no action arises from a base cause – but a trespasser is not outside protection entirely (Bird v Holbrook, 1828, spring-gun without notice).
Contributory negligence reduces damages proportionately; India follows apportionment (e.g. Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay v Laxman Iyer, 2003).

steps.title: Problem
steps.body:
A cricket spectator is hit by a ball struck to the boundary in a normal shot.
1. Inherent risk of the game → implied consent.
2. No negligence by organiser beyond normal risk → volenti succeeds.
Variant: the ball hits a fan because the stadium's protective net was torn for weeks → negligence beyond accepted risk; volenti fails.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using volenti against a rescuer: rescue is a natural response to the defendant's wrong, so it is not voluntary assumption of risk.

lessons.title: Inevitable accident, act of God and necessity

scenes.text: In Nichols v Marsland (1876) an extraordinary rainstorm burst artificial lakes and destroyed bridges.
The defendant was not liable: the rain was an act of God.

steps.title: Inevitable accident
steps.body: An accident that could not have been avoided by reasonable care and skill. Stanley v Powell (1891): pellet ricocheted from a tree and hit the plaintiff; no negligence → no liability. Brown v Kendall (1850). Holmes v Mather (1875): horses bolted despite care.

steps.title: Act of God (vis major)
steps.body:
Operation of natural forces so unexpected that no human foresight could provide against it. Needs (1) natural forces and (2) extraordinary occurrence.
Cases: Nichols v Marsland; Ramalinga Nadar v Narayana Reddiar (1971) – mob looting held not act of God (human agency); Kallu Lal v Hemchand (1958) – ordinary rain causing wall collapse not act of God.

steps.title: Necessity, private defence, mistake, statutory authority
steps.body:
- Necessity: harm caused to prevent greater harm (Cope v Sharpe, 1912, fire-break; Leigh v Gladstone, 1909, force-feeding)
- Private defence: reasonable force to protect person or property (Bird v Holbrook – excessive spring-gun not allowed)
- Mistake: generally not a defence (Consolidated Co. v Curtis, 1892), though relevant for malicious prosecution and false imprisonment in some cases
- Statutory authority: act authorised by statute is a defence if done without negligence (Vaughan v Taff Vale Railway, 1860; Hammersmith Rail Co v Brand, 1869)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Confusing the two: act of God needs natural forces; inevitable accident may be any event unavoidable by reasonable care.

story.title: Who can sue, who can be sued?

scenes.text: A 12-year-old throws a stone and breaks a car window.
A minor can be liable in tort; parents are not automatically liable unless they were negligent or the child acted as their agent.

steps.title: Capacity
steps.body:
- Minors: liable for torts where the required mental element exists; parents liable only for their own negligence or authority
- Persons of unsound mind: may be liable unless the mental element required is absent
- Corporations: liable for torts of servants in course of business
- State: liable subject to sovereign immunity issues (Unit 3)
- Foreign sovereigns and diplomats: immunity
- Husband and wife: can sue each other under modern law

steps.title: Joint tortfeasors
steps.body: Where two or more persons act in concert (common design, agency, vicarious liability), each is liable for the whole damage. Independent tortfeasors causing the same damage may also be liable jointly and severally. Contribution among tortfeasors is allowed in India on equitable principles.

steps.title: Discharge of tort liability
steps.body: Death (actio personalis moritur cum persona, modified by the Legal Representatives' Suits Act 1855 and the Fatal Accidents Act 1855), waiver by election, accord and satisfaction, release, judgment, limitation (Limitation Act 1963, e.g. one year for defamation, three years for most compensation claims).

courses.title: Unit 2 · Negligence
courses.summary: Duty of care from Donoghue v Stevenson to Caparo, breach and the reasonable person, causation and remoteness (Re Polemis, The Wagon Mound), res ipsa loquitur, professional and medical negligence (Bolam, Jacob Mathew), nervous shock, and contributory negligence with apportionment.

scenes.text: In 1928 Mrs Donoghue drank ginger beer bought by a friend; a decomposed snail was in the opaque bottle.
In Donoghue v Stevenson (1932) Lord Atkin's 'neighbour principle' let her sue the manufacturer though she had no contract.

steps.title: Elements of negligence
steps.body:
1. Duty of care owed by defendant to plaintiff
2. Breach of that duty
3. Consequential damage that is not too remote
Neighbour principle: you must take reasonable care to avoid acts or omissions which you can reasonably foresee would be likely to injure your neighbour – persons so closely and directly affected that you ought reasonably to have them in contemplation.

steps.title: Caparo three-stage test
steps.body:
Caparo Industries v Dickman (1990): (1) reasonable foreseeability of harm; (2) proximity of relationship; (3) fair, just and reasonable to impose a duty.
Anns v Merton (1978) two-stage test was departed from in Murphy v Brentwood (1991). Indian courts use foreseeability and proximity, often citing Donoghue and Caparo.

steps.title: Special duty situations
steps.body:
- Pure economic loss: generally not recoverable except Hedley Byrne v Heller (1964) negligent misstatement with assumption of responsibility
- Omissions: no general duty to rescue
- Nervous shock: primary victims; secondary victims need close tie of love, proximity in time and space, and perception by own senses (Alcock v Chief Constable, 1992)
- Unborn children and rescuers can be owed duties

steps.title: Problem
steps.body:
A tea-stall owner leaves a gas cylinder leaking near a bus stop; a passer-by is burned.
1. Foreseeable: leaking gas near a crowd → fire risk is obvious.
2. Proximity: passers-by at the bus stop are directly affected.
3. Fair, just, reasonable: yes.
Duty exists; next ask breach and causation.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Jumping to breach without first establishing duty, or treating duty as owed to the whole world in every case.

scenes.text: Oil spilled from The Wagon Mound into Sydney Harbour; welding sparks later ignited it and the wharf burned.
The Privy Council (1961) held the fire damage too remote because it was not reasonably foreseeable.

steps.title: Breach – the reasonable person
steps.body:
Blyth v Birmingham Waterworks (1856): negligence is the omission to do something a reasonable man would do.
Factors: probability of harm (Bolton v Stone, 1951 – cricket ball rarely left the ground: no breach); seriousness (Paris v Stepney, 1951 – one-eyed worker: goggles needed); cost and practicality of precautions (Latimer v AEC, 1953); social utility (Watt v Hertfordshire, 1954 – fire service rescue).

steps.title: Causation
steps.body:
But-for test: would the harm have happened but for the breach? Barnett v Chelsea and Kensington Hospital (1969): doctor failed to examine, but the patient would have died of arsenic anyway → no causation.
Novus actus interveniens: a free, deliberate, unreasonable intervening act may break the chain (The Oropesa, 1943 – not broken).

steps.title: Remoteness
steps.body:
Re Polemis (1921): directness test – liable for all direct consequences.
The Wagon Mound (No. 1) (1961): foreseeability of the kind of damage.
Hughes v Lord Advocate (1963): if the type of harm is foreseeable, the exact manner need not be.
Eggshell-skull rule: take your victim as you find him (Smith v Leech Brain, 1962).

steps.title: Problem
steps.body:
A driver speeds and hits B, causing a minor cut. B has a rare blood disorder and suffers serious complications.
Breach: speeding. Causation: but for the collision, no cut. Remoteness: personal injury was foreseeable; eggshell-skull rule → liable for the full extent.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Applying Re Polemis as current law: The Wagon Mound replaced directness with foreseeability.

lessons.title: Res ipsa loquitur and medical negligence

scenes.text: After an abdominal surgery, a patient keeps having pain; an X-ray shows a surgical mop inside.
The thing speaks for itself: the hospital must explain how this could happen without negligence.

steps.title: Res ipsa loquitur
steps.body:
Scott v London and St Katherine Docks (1865): sugar bags fell from a warehouse.
Conditions: (1) the thing was under the defendant's management or control; (2) the accident is such as does not ordinarily happen if proper care is used; (3) no explanation of the cause is available.
Effect: raises an inference of negligence; the defendant must rebut. Indian cases: Municipal Corporation of Delhi v Subhagwanti (1966) – clock tower collapse.

steps.title: Medical negligence
steps.body:
Bolam v Friern Hospital (1957): a doctor is not negligent if he acts in accordance with a practice accepted as proper by a responsible body of medical opinion.
Bolitho (1997): that opinion must withstand logical analysis.
Jacob Mathew v State of Punjab (2005): Bolam applies in India; for criminal liability, negligence must be gross; guidelines on prosecution of doctors.
V. Kishan Rao v Nikhil Super Speciality Hospital (2010): expert evidence not mandatory in every case where res ipsa applies.
Indian Medical Association v V.P. Shantha (1995): medical services for a fee are 'services' under consumer law.

steps.title: Problem
steps.body:
A doctor prescribes a drug following standard guidelines; the patient has a rare reaction not listed.
Bolam: responsible medical opinion supports the choice → no negligence.
Variant: doctor prescribes 10 times the normal dose by mistake → breach obvious; res ipsa may apply.

steps.title: Apportionment
steps.body:
Older common law made contributory negligence a complete defence (Butterfield v Forrester, 1809); 'last opportunity' rule (Davies v Mann, 1842).
Modern rule (Law Reform (Contributory Negligence) Act 1945 in England; adopted on equitable grounds in India): damages reduced to the extent the court thinks just. Froom v Butcher (1976): seat-belt reductions. Composite negligence (two defendants, innocent plaintiff) – no reduction; plaintiff can recover the whole from either.

steps.title: Worked numeric
steps.body:
Total loss assessed = ₹8,00,000. Plaintiff's share of fault = 25%.
Award = 8,00,000 × (1 − 0.25) = 8,00,000 × 0.75 = ₹6,00,000.

steps.title: Multiplier method (Motor accident claims)
steps.body:
Sarla Verma (2009) and Pranay Sethi (2017) use: annual income × (1 + future prospects) × (1 − personal expenses deduction) × multiplier.
Deceased aged 30, salaried, monthly income ₹30,000, 3 dependants.
Annual = 3,60,000; future prospects 40% (below 40, permanent job) → 5,04,000; deduction 1/3 for 2–3 dependants → 3,36,000; multiplier for age 26–30 = 17.
Loss of dependency = 3,36,000 × 17 = ₹57,12,000 (plus conventional heads).

courses.summary: Public and private nuisance; the rule in Rylands v Fletcher with its exceptions; absolute liability in M.C. Mehta (Oleum gas) and the Bhopal context; vicarious liability of masters and employers; and State liability from Kasturi Lal to Nilabati Behera and constitutional torts.

scenes.text: A flour mill runs through the night beside a residential area. Neighbours cannot sleep.
Private nuisance: an unreasonable interference with the use or enjoyment of land.

steps.title: Kinds
steps.body:
**Public nuisance**: an act affecting the public at large (obstruction of a highway). A private person can sue only if he suffers special damage beyond the public. Also a crime and remediable by s.91 CPC and by the magistrate under the BNSS.
**Private nuisance**: unlawful interference with a person's use or enjoyment of land, or some right over it.
Essentials: unreasonable interference; interference with use or enjoyment of land; damage (actual or presumed in some cases).

steps.title: Reasonableness factors
steps.body:
Locality (Sturges v Bridgman, 1879 – 'what would be a nuisance in Belgrave Square would not necessarily be so in Bermondsey'), duration, sensitivity of plaintiff (Robinson v Kilvert, 1889 – abnormally sensitive paper, no nuisance), malice (Christie v Davey, 1893; Hollywood Silver Fox Farm v Emmett, 1936).
Indian: Radhey Shyam v Gur Prasad (1978) – flour mill noise in a residential area; Ram Baj Singh v Babulal (1982) – brick kiln dust.

steps.title: Defences
steps.body:
Valid: prescription (20 years in English law; easement by prescription in India under the Limitation Act/Easements Act), statutory authority.
Not valid: coming to the nuisance (Sturges v Bridgman), public benefit, that many people contributed, reasonable care taken.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Saying an individual can always sue for public nuisance: special damage is necessary.
