story.title: A reservoir over old mine shafts

scenes.text: Fletcher's independent contractors built a reservoir; water flooded Rylands' neighbour's mine through old shafts.
The House of Lords (1868) held the owner liable without negligence.

steps.title: Rule (Blackburn J)
steps.body:
A person who for his own purposes brings on his land and collects and keeps there anything likely to do mischief if it escapes must keep it at his peril; if he does not, he is prima facie answerable for all damage which is the natural consequence of its escape.
Elements: (1) dangerous thing; (2) brought on land and kept; (3) non-natural use (Lord Cairns); (4) escape (Read v Lyons, 1947 – no escape, no liability).

steps.title: Exceptions
steps.body:
1. Plaintiff's own default (Ponting v Noakes, 1894)
2. Act of God (Nichols v Marsland)
3. Consent of the plaintiff / common benefit
4. Act of a stranger (Box v Jubb, 1879)
5. Statutory authority (Green v Chelsea Waterworks, 1894)
Cambridge Water v Eastern Counties Leather (1994): foreseeability of the type of damage is required.

steps.title: Problem
steps.body:
A firm stores fireworks in a residential godown; an unknown trespasser sets fire, the stock explodes and damages houses.
Elements satisfied; exception: act of a stranger may apply under Rylands, unless the firm could foresee and prevent it. Under Indian absolute liability (next lesson), no such exception.

steps.title: The rule
steps.body:
An enterprise engaged in a hazardous or inherently dangerous industry which poses a potential threat to health and safety owes an absolute and non-delegable duty to the community to ensure no harm results. If harm results, it is absolutely liable – none of the Rylands exceptions apply.
Compensation must correlate with the magnitude and capacity of the enterprise (deterrent effect).

steps.title: Master and servant
steps.body:
Qui facit per alium facit per se. The employer is liable for torts of employees committed in the **course of employment** – wrongful authorised acts or wrongful and unauthorised modes of doing authorised acts (Salmond).
Cases: Century Insurance v Northern Ireland Road Transport (1942) – smoking while unloading petrol; Lloyd v Grace Smith (1912) – clerk's fraud; Limpus v London General Omnibus (1862) – prohibited racing; State Bank of India v Shyama Devi (1978) – employee's private dealing outside course.
Independent contractors: generally no liability, except non-delegable duties or hazardous work.
Lister v Hesley Hall (2001): close connection test.

steps.title: State liability
steps.body:
Art. 300: Union and States can sue and be sued as the East India Company could.
- P&O Steam Navigation v Secretary of State (1861): sovereign vs non-sovereign functions
- State of Rajasthan v Vidyawati (1962): State liable for negligent driving of a government jeep (non-sovereign)
- Kasturi Lal (1965): immunity for sovereign functions
- Rudul Sah (1983): compensation under Art. 32 for illegal detention
- Nilabati Behera (1993): custodial death; sovereign immunity no defence in public law compensation for violation of Fundamental Rights
- N. Nagendra Rao (1997): doctrine of sovereign immunity largely outdated

scenes.text: A shopkeeper suspects a customer of theft and locks her in a back room for two hours.
Total restraint of liberty without lawful justification is false imprisonment, even if no force is used.

steps.title: Assault and battery
steps.body:
**Assault**: an act causing reasonable apprehension of immediate unlawful force (Stephens v Myers, 1830 – advancing with clenched fist). Words can also negate a threat (Tuberville v Savage, 1669 – 'if it were not assize-time').
**Battery**: intentional application of force to another without lawful justification, however slight (Cole v Turner, 1704). Spitting on a person is battery. Hostility is not always needed.

steps.title: False imprisonment
steps.body:
Total restraint on liberty, without lawful justification, for any period. Knowledge of the plaintiff not necessary (Meering v Grahame-White Aviation, 1919). Partial obstruction is not enough (Bird v Jones, 1845).
Indian: Bhim Singh (1985); Rudul Sah (1983) – detention for 14 years after acquittal.

steps.title: Malicious prosecution
steps.body: Essentials: (1) prosecution by the defendant; (2) without reasonable and probable cause; (3) with malice; (4) terminated in plaintiff's favour; (5) damage. West Bengal State Electricity Board v Dilip Kumar Ray (2007) restated these.

steps.title: Problem
steps.body:
A guard raises a stick and runs at a boy, who flees; the guard misses.
Assault: reasonable apprehension of immediate force – yes.
Battery: no contact – no.
If the guard catches and slaps him → battery as well.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Requiring physical locks for false imprisonment: restraint by threat or show of authority is enough.

items.text: Pointing a loaded gun at someone nearby
Spitting on a person
Locking a guest in a room
Pushing a person aside roughly

quiz.why: Meering v Grahame-White held that a person can be falsely imprisoned without knowing it.

options: Partial obstruction is not false imprisonment
quiz.why: The plaintiff could go another way, so the restraint was not total.

quiz.why: The earlier proceedings must have ended in favour of the plaintiff.

lessons.title: Trespass to land, trespass to goods and conversion

scenes.text: A man parks his car on his neighbour's private driveway every day without permission.
Trespass to land is actionable per se – no damage needed.

steps.title: Trespass to land
steps.body:
Unjustifiable interference with possession of land: entering, remaining, placing objects. Actionable per se. Airspace up to a reasonable height and subsoil are included. Trespass ab initio: entry under legal authority later abused (Six Carpenters' Case, 1610).
Remedies: damages, injunction, re-entry by reasonable force, mesne profits.

steps.title: Goods
steps.body:
**Trespass to goods**: wrongful direct interference with possession.
**Conversion**: dealing with goods in a manner inconsistent with the owner's right, e.g. selling, destroying, refusing to return (Hollins v Fowler, 1875).
**Detinue**: wrongful detention after demand; remedy is return of the goods or their value.

steps.title: Problem
steps.body:
A borrows B's bicycle for a day and sells it to C.
A: conversion – selling is inconsistent with B's ownership.
C, even if innocent, may be liable in conversion if he refuses to return it after demand.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Requiring proof of damage for trespass: it is actionable per se.

items.text: Walking across a farm without permission
Selling a borrowed phone
Keeping a borrowed book after the owner demands it

quiz.q: Trespass to land is actionable
quiz.why: No proof of damage is needed because the right to possession itself is protected.

quiz.q: Six Carpenters' Case concerned
quiz.why: Abuse of a lawful entry can make the entry trespass from the beginning.

quiz.q: Selling another's goods without authority is
quiz.why: It is dealing that denies the owner's title.

scenes.text: A newspaper reports that a named contractor bribed officials. It cannot prove it.
Truth is a complete defence in civil defamation; without it the paper may pay damages.

steps.title: Essentials
steps.body:
1. Statement is defamatory – tends to lower the plaintiff in the estimation of right-thinking members of society (Sim v Stretch, 1936)
2. It refers to the plaintiff (Newstead v London Express, 1940; Hulton v Jones, 1910 – unintended reference)
3. It is published to at least one person other than the plaintiff (Mahendra Ram v Harnandan Prasad, 1958 – Urdu letter read by a third person because the plaintiff could not read Urdu)
Innuendo: an apparently innocent statement with a hidden defamatory meaning (Tolley v Fry, 1931).

steps.title: Libel vs slander
steps.body:
Libel: permanent form (writing, print, film, broadcast). Slander: transient (spoken words, gestures).
English law: libel actionable per se; slander needs special damage except in listed categories. In India, both are generally treated as actionable per se in civil law, and defamation is also an offence (BNS 2023 s.356, earlier s.499 IPC; upheld in Subramanian Swamy v Union of India, 2016).

steps.title: Defences
steps.body:
- **Justification/truth**: complete defence in civil law
- **Fair comment**: on matters of public interest; comment, not fact; honest
- **Absolute privilege**: Parliamentary proceedings (Arts. 105, 194), judicial proceedings
- **Qualified privilege**: duty and interest, without malice – e.g. employer's reference
- R. Rajagopal v State of TN (1994): public officials cannot sue for publications about acts in official duty unless the publisher acted with reckless disregard for truth
- Apology/consent

steps.title: Problem
steps.body:
A blogger writes 'Dr X's hospital killed my father through greed'. The father died of a known complication; no greed was proved.
1. Defamatory: yes (imputes professional misconduct).
2. Refers to Dr X: named.
3. Published online.
Defences: truth fails; fair comment fails as it states a fact without basis. Liability likely.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Saying intention to defame is required: Hulton v Jones shows unintended reference can be enough.

items.text: MP's speech in Lok Sabha
Honest film review calling a movie dull
Accurate report that a person was convicted
Former employer's honest reference letter

quiz.why: Libel is in a permanent form such as print or broadcast.

quiz.why: The Supreme Court upheld ss.499–500 IPC as reasonable restrictions.

quiz.why: Articles 105 and 194 give members absolute immunity for what they say in the House.

quiz.q: Hulton v Jones shows
quiz.why: A fictional name matched a real person, and the paper was held liable.

scenes.text: A builder starts demolishing your compound wall by mistake.
You need a quick court order to stop it, then damages for what is broken.

steps.title: Damages
steps.body:
- Nominal: right violated, no loss (Ashby v White)
- Contemptuous: tiny sum showing disapproval of the claim
- Compensatory (general and special)
- Aggravated: for injured feelings
- Exemplary/punitive: to punish (Rookes v Barnard, 1964 categories; used by Indian courts in constitutional torts and in M.C. Mehta v Kamal Nath)
Restitutio in integrum: put the plaintiff in the position as if the tort had not occurred.

steps.title: Injunctions
steps.body:
Temporary (Order 39 CPC): prima facie case, balance of convenience, irreparable injury.
Perpetual (s.38 Specific Relief Act). Mandatory (s.39). Quia timet: to prevent apprehended harm.

steps.title: Extra-judicial remedies
steps.body: Self-defence, expulsion of a trespasser with reasonable force, re-entry on land, recaption of goods, abatement of nuisance, distress damage feasant.

steps.title: Computing a claim
steps.body: Accident claim: medical bills ₹1,20,000; lost wages ₹60,000 (special damages); pain and suffering assessed ₹1,00,000 (general). Total = 1,20,000 + 60,000 + 1,00,000 = ₹2,80,000. With 20% contributory fault: 2,80,000 × 0.8 = ₹2,24,000.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Confusing nominal damages (a right violated, no loss) with contemptuous damages (disapproval of a technically valid claim).

items.text: Stop an ongoing demolition pending trial
Punish police for deliberate custodial torture
Harmless trespass proved

quiz.why: They must be specifically pleaded and proved, like bills and lost wages.

options: Prima facie case, balance of convenience, irreparable injury
quiz.why: These three tests guide courts under Order 39 CPC.

quiz.why: The total of ₹1,50,000 reduced by 10% gives ₹1,35,000.

courses.title: Unit 5 · Consumer Protection Act 2019
courses.summary: Who is a consumer, goods, services, defect, deficiency and unfair trade practice under the Consumer Protection Act 2019; consumer rights and the Central Consumer Protection Authority; the three-tier Commissions with pecuniary jurisdiction, complaint procedure, limitation and appeals; mediation; product liability (Chapter VI); and e-commerce rules.
outcomes: Decide whether a person is a 'consumer' including the commercial-purpose exclusion
Identify defect, deficiency and unfair trade practice in facts
Choose the correct Commission by pecuniary jurisdiction and compute limitation
Explain the role of the CCPA and mediation
Apply product liability of manufacturer, service provider and seller

lessons.title: Consumer, goods, services and key definitions

story.title: A builder who delayed for six years

scenes.text: A homebuyer booked a flat in 2016 with possession promised in 2019; by 2025 there is still no flat.
Housing construction is a 'service', and delay is a deficiency – the buyer can approach a Consumer Commission.

steps.title: Consumer – s.2(7)
steps.body:
A person who buys goods or hires or avails of services for consideration paid, promised or partly paid, including deferred payment, and includes beneficiaries/users with approval. Includes offline and online transactions, teleshopping, direct selling, multi-level marketing.
Excludes a person who obtains goods for resale or for any commercial purpose – but 'commercial purpose' does not include use by a person for earning his livelihood by means of self-employment (Laxmi Engineering Works v PSG Industrial Institute, 1995).

steps.title: Other definitions
steps.body:
- Defect (s.2(10)): fault, imperfection or shortcoming in quality, quantity, potency, purity or standard of goods
- Deficiency (s.2(11)): fault or inadequacy in quality, nature and manner of performance of services; includes negligence or deliberate withholding of relevant information
- Service (s.2(42)): includes banking, insurance, transport, housing construction, entertainment, etc.; excludes free services and contracts of personal service
- Unfair trade practice (s.2(47)): false representations, misleading ads, not issuing a bill, refusing to take back defective goods within 30 days, disclosing personal information
- Misleading advertisement (s.2(28)); endorser liability

steps.title: Who is a consumer?
steps.body:
1. A taxi driver buys one car to drive himself for living → consumer (self-employment).
2. A company buys 50 laptops for its offices → commercial purpose; generally not a consumer.
3. A patient treated free at a government hospital where all are treated free → not 'service' for consideration (V.P. Shantha distinctions).
4. A homebuyer of a flat for residence → consumer.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Saying any business buyer is excluded: the self-employment livelihood exception keeps small buyers in.

items.text: Shopkeeper buying stock to resell
Tailor buying one sewing machine to earn a livelihood
Student paying for coaching classes
Employee claiming against employer under service contract

quiz.why: The Explanation to s.2(7) and Laxmi Engineering keep such users as consumers.

quiz.why: Section 2(47) lists it as an unfair trade practice.

scenes.text: A soap brand claims '100% protection from all germs' with no proof.
The Central Consumer Protection Authority can order the ad withdrawn and impose penalties on the manufacturer and endorser.

steps.title: Six consumer rights (s.2(9))
steps.body:
1. Right to be protected against hazardous goods and services
2. Right to be informed about quality, quantity, potency, purity, standard and price
3. Right to access a variety of goods and services at competitive prices
4. Right to be heard
5. Right to seek redressal
6. Right to consumer awareness

steps.title: CCPA (Chapter III)
steps.body:
Established under s.10 to protect and enforce rights of consumers as a class. Powers: inquiry and investigation, recall of goods, refund, discontinuing unfair practices, directions on misleading advertisements, filing complaints.
Penalty for misleading ads (s.21): up to ₹10 lakh for manufacturer or endorser, up to ₹50 lakh for subsequent contravention; endorser may be prohibited from endorsing for up to one year (three years for subsequent). Endorser defence: due diligence.

steps.title: Consumer Protection Councils
steps.body: Central, State and District Councils are advisory bodies promoting consumer rights (Chapter II).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Saying the CCPA decides individual compensation claims: individual complaints go to the Commissions; the CCPA deals with class-wide violations.

items: Order recall of unsafe goods
Order refund of price to consumers
Direct discontinuance of a misleading ad
Impose penalties on endorsers
Conduct investigations through its investigation wing

quiz.why: Section 10 of the 2019 Act.

quiz.why: Up to ₹10 lakh for the first contravention.

quiz.why: Section 2(9) lists it.

scenes.text: A buyer paid ₹65 lakh for a flat that was never delivered.
Pecuniary jurisdiction is based on the value of goods or services paid as consideration.

steps.title: Pecuniary jurisdiction (as revised by the 2021 Rules)
steps.body:
Under the Consumer Protection (Jurisdiction of the District Commission, the State Commission and the National Commission) Rules 2021:
- District Commission: consideration paid up to ₹50 lakh
- State Commission: above ₹50 lakh up to ₹2 crore
- National Commission (NCDRC): above ₹2 crore
(The Act's original figures were ₹1 crore and ₹10 crore; the 2021 Rules lowered them.)
Territorial: where the opposite party resides or works, or where the cause of action arises, or where the complainant resides or works (s.34(2)(d)) – a 2019 addition. E-filing is permitted.

steps.title: Procedure
steps.body:
- Who can file (s.35): consumer, recognised consumer association, one or more consumers with same interest (class), Central/State Government, CCPA
- Limitation (s.69): within 2 years from the date the cause of action arises, extendable for sufficient cause
- Admissibility to be decided ordinarily within 21 days; deemed admitted if not decided
- Disposal target: 3 months where no testing of goods is needed, 5 months where testing is needed
- Reliefs (s.39): remove defect, replace, refund, compensation, punitive damages, discontinue unfair trade practice, corrective advertisement

steps.title: Appeals
steps.body:
District → State Commission within 45 days (s.41); deposit of 50% of the amount ordered.
State → National within 30 days (s.51); 50% deposit.
National → Supreme Court within 30 days (s.67); 50% deposit.
Orders enforceable; non-compliance punishable (s.72) with imprisonment from 1 month to 3 years and/or fine ₹25,000 to ₹1 lakh.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
1. Flat price paid ₹65 lakh → above ₹50 lakh, up to ₹2 crore → State Commission.
2. Possession due 31 March 2024; cause of action continuing for non-delivery, but take the outer date: complaint by 30 March 2026 to be safe.
3. Commission orders ₹80 lakh refund with interest; builder appeals to NCDRC → must deposit 50% = ₹40 lakh.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using the Act's original ₹1 crore / ₹10 crore limits without noting the 2021 Rules.

scenes.text: A new pressure cooker explodes because of a manufacturing defect, injuring a user.
Chapter VI of the 2019 Act makes the manufacturer liable even without proof of negligence.

steps.title: Product liability (ss.82–87)
steps.body:
Product liability action for harm caused by a defective product, against a product manufacturer, product service provider or product seller.
s.84 – manufacturer liable for manufacturing defect, design defect, deviation from specifications, non-conformity to express warranty, inadequate instructions/warnings – even if not negligent or fraudulent in making the express warranty.
s.85 – service provider liable for faulty, imperfect or deficient service, negligence, inadequate instructions.
s.86 – seller liable in limited cases: exercised substantial control, altered the product, made its own express warranty, manufacturer not identifiable or not amenable to process.
s.87 – exceptions: misuse, alteration, adequate warnings given, obvious or commonly known dangers.

steps.title: Mediation (Chapter V)
steps.body: With consent of both parties, the Commission may refer the dispute to mediation through consumer mediation cells; settlement is recorded and becomes an order. No appeal lies against an order passed on a mediated settlement.

steps.title: E-commerce
steps.body: Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules 2020: e-commerce entities must display seller details, return/refund policies, country of origin; appoint a grievance officer, acknowledge complaints within 48 hours and redress within one month; no manipulation of prices or fake reviews; marketplace and inventory models regulated.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Saying a retailer is always liable as a seller: s.86 limits seller liability to specific situations.
